```{r setup}
    return(paste0("Some Session 4 logs could not be read, which removed further judgements ",
                  "**[Check: the input-gap census no longer matches the ",
                  "two features and the one session this sentence describes]**."))
  }
  n_of <- function(reason) length(unique(.gap_tbl$participant_lab_ID[.gap_tbl$reason == reason]))
  # Counts below ten are spelled out, as APA 7 asks of counts in running text.
  num_word <- function(n) {
    if (n >= 1 && n <= 9) c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven",
                            "eight", "nine")[n] else format(n, big.mark = ",")
  }
  sprintf(paste0(
    "Two features of the Session 4 logs removed further judgements. ",
    "The runs of %s participants were exported in two files whose names the extraction's ",
    "file pattern does not match, and the logs of %s participants were exported with a ",
    "semicolon delimiter that the comma-delimited reader cannot parse. Those participants ",
    "contribute no Session 4 judgements and enter the models through their other sessions ",
    "only."), num_word(n_of("split_export")), num_word(n_of("semicolon_delimited")))
}

# --- Extents of the FDR-surviving clusters in a pooled decoding time-course ---
# Typed cluster extents would go stale the moment the decoding is re-run (the
# B = 1000 rerun can shift cluster boundaries), so they are read back from the
# artefact. Returned in temporal order.
dec_fdr_spans <- function(prop) {
  d <- decode_tc[[prop]]
  if (is.null(d) || !"cluster_p_fdr" %in% names(d)) return(character(0))
  ov <- d[d$analysis == "overall" & !is.na(d$cluster_id) &
            !is.na(d$cluster_p_fdr) & d$cluster_p_fdr < .05, , drop = FALSE]
  if (!nrow(ov)) return(character(0))
  sp <- lapply(split(ov$time_ms, ov$cluster_id), range)
  sp <- sp[order(vapply(sp, `[`, 0, 1))]
  vapply(sp, function(x) sprintf("%s to %s ms", .dec_ms(x[1]), .dec_ms(x[2])), "")
}
dec_span <- function(prop, i) {
  s <- dec_fdr_spans(prop)
  if (length(s) < i) return("*[pending decoding run]*")
  s[i]
}
# Smallest cluster-level p of one property, formatted as a p value (leading zero dropped,
# "< .001" below .001, as APA style has it and as the floor 1/(B + 1) is stated in the
# Method). `field` is "min_clp" for every analysis of the property and "min_clp_overall"
# for its pooled overall time-course alone, which is what a sentence about that
# time-course must use.
dec_min_p <- function(s, field = "min_clp") {
  v <- if (is.null(s)) NULL else s[[field]]
  if (is.null(v) || is.na(v)) return("*[pending decoding run]*")
  if (v < .001) return("$p < .001$")
  paste0("$p = ", sub("^0", "", formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 3)), "$")
}
# Whether that smallest cluster-level p sits exactly at the permutation floor 1/(B + 1).
# A p at the floor is indistinguishable from any smaller value, so a null resting on it
# reports the resolution of the null as much as it reports the data. Emitted from the
# artefact so the clause disappears by itself once a larger null separates the two.
dec_at_floor <- function(s, field = "min_clp") {
  b <- .n_perm_conf()
  v <- if (is.null(s)) NULL else s[[field]]
  if (is.null(v) || is.na(v) || all(is.na(b)) || length(b) > 1) return("")
  if (!isTRUE(all.equal(unname(v), 1 / (b + 1)))) return("")
  ", which is the smallest value the permutation null can return"
}
# How many clusters of a property's pooled overall time-course sit at that floor. Counted
# from the artefact so the disclosure tracks the run rather than a typed recollection.
dec_n_at_floor <- function(prop) {
  d <- decode_tc[[prop]]; b <- .n_perm_conf()
  if (is.null(d) || all(is.na(b)) || length(b) > 1) return("*[pending decoding run]*")
  ov <- unique(d[d$analysis == "overall" & !is.na(d$cluster_id),
                 c("cluster_id", "cluster_p"), drop = FALSE])
  n <- sum(abs(ov$cluster_p - 1 / (b + 1)) < 1e-9, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (n > 9L) return(as.character(n))
  c("none", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight",
    "nine")[n + 1L]
}

# --- Render-time guard for prose that names WHICH cells are credible ----------
# cred_cells() injects the count of credible cells, but sentences also describe
# their location ("both on the midline", "every one of those cells is lateral").
# A refit can change the credible set while those words stand, a drift invisible
# at render time. This guard compares the credible set against the cells the
# sentence names and prints a visible marker on any mismatch, mirroring
# misfilter_status().
cred_cells_guard <- function(term, expected, property = "",
                             structure = if (identical(LES_P1_PRIMARY, "maximal")) "itemslope" else "base",
                             tbl = post_tbl) {
  if (is.null(tbl)) return("")
  # Same bucketing rule as cred_cells(): the retention-free refits belong to neither
  # structure, so they are excluded before the base/maximal split.
  is_item <- grepl("_itemslope$", tbl$model)
  k <- tbl$parameter == term & grepl(paste0("^erp_", property), tbl$model) &
       !.is_variant(tbl$model) & (if (structure == "itemslope") is_item else !is_item)
  d <- tbl[k, , drop = FALSE]
  if (!nrow(d)) return("")
  got <- sort(sub("_itemslope$", "", d$model[d$ci_low > 0 | d$ci_high < 0]))
  if (identical(got, sort(unique(expected)))) return("")
  paste0(" **[Check: the credible set for this term is now {",
         paste(got, collapse = ", "),
         "}; the surrounding sentence names a different set and must be updated.]**")
}

# Signed credible set of one term in one family of ERP fits: the bare cell ids whose
# interval excludes zero, each tagged with the sign of its median. `suffix` is what follows
# the cell id in that family's model ids ("_itemslope" for the maximal fits, "" for the base
# ones, "_weakprior_itemslope", "_exclreproc_itemslope"), and the anchored pattern keeps
# the other families out. NULL when the family is absent.
.cred_set <- function(term, suffix, tbl = post_tbl) {
  if (is.null(tbl)) return(NULL)
  d <- tbl[tbl$parameter == term &
             grepl(paste0("^erp_.*_(lateral|midline)", suffix, "$"), tbl$model), , drop = FALSE]
  if (!nrow(d)) return(NULL)
  k <- d$ci_low > 0 | d$ci_high < 0
  sort(paste0(sub(paste0(suffix, "$"), "", d$model[k]), ifelse(d$median[k] > 0, " (+)", " (-)")))
}

# Sentences that compare two families of fits ("the same cells are credible under the weak
# priors", "every credible term keeps its sign without the reprocessed records") are checked
# here, term by term over the four grammaticality terms: the terms whose signed credible sets
# differ between `suffix` and `reference` must be exactly those named in `differ`. A
# mismatch, or an absent family, prints a visible marker, as cred_cells_guard() does.
cred_agree_guard <- function(suffix, reference = .STRUCT_SUFFIX[[LES_P1_PRIMARY]],
                             differ = character(), tbl = post_tbl) {
  if (is.null(tbl)) return("")
  terms <- c("z_recoded_grammaticality",
             "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language",
             "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session",
             "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")
  a <- lapply(terms, .cred_set, suffix = suffix, tbl = tbl)
  b <- lapply(terms, .cred_set, suffix = reference, tbl = tbl)
  if (any(vapply(c(a, b), is.null, logical(1))))
    return(paste0(" **[Pending: the fits compared here (\"", suffix, "\" against \"",
                  reference, "\") are not all in the pooled summaries.]**"))
  got <- terms[!mapply(identical, a, b)]
  if (setequal(got, differ)) return("")
  paste0(" **[Check: the credible sets now differ for {", paste(.pretty_term(got), collapse = "; "),
         "}; the surrounding sentence says otherwise and must be updated.]**")
}

# The counterpart of cred_cells_guard() for the retention contrasts: the bare cell ids whose
# `contrast` is credible, in the primary structure's fits, or in its retention-free refits
# when `freed` is TRUE, must be those the sentence names.
ret_cred_guard <- function(contrast, expected, property = "", freed = FALSE,
                           tbl = retention_tbl) {
  if (is.null(tbl)) return("")
  suffix <- paste0(.STRUCT_SUFFIX[[LES_P1_PRIMARY]], if (freed) "_retfree" else "")
  d <- tbl[tbl$contrast == contrast &
             grepl(paste0("^erp_", property, ".*_(lateral|midline)", suffix, "$"), tbl$model), ,
           drop = FALSE]
  if (!nrow(d)) return("")
  got <- sort(sub(paste0(suffix, "$"), "", d$model[d$ci_low > 0 | d$ci_high < 0]))
  if (identical(got, sort(unique(expected)))) return("")
  paste0(" **[Check: the credible set for this contrast is now {",
         paste(got, collapse = ", "),
         "}; the surrounding sentence names a different set and must be updated.]**")
}

# The robustness rule applied to the Session 4 to 6 contrasts: every contrast credible in
# the primary fits must stay credible, with the same sign, without the reprocessed and
# recovered records, and the contrasts that become credible only there must be exactly
# `extra` ("<cell id> <contrast>"), which the sentence names as not claimable.
ret_robust_guard <- function(extra = character(), tbl = retention_tbl) {
  if (is.null(tbl)) return("")
  .signed <- function(suffix) {
    d <- tbl[grepl(paste0("^erp_.*_(lateral|midline)", suffix, "$"), tbl$model), , drop = FALSE]
    k <- d$ci_low > 0 | d$ci_high < 0
    list(n = nrow(d), key = paste(sub(paste0(suffix, "$"), "", d$model[k]), d$contrast[k]),
         sign = sign(d$median[k]))
  }
  p <- .signed("_itemslope"); r <- .signed("_exclreproc_itemslope")
  if (!p$n || !r$n) return(" **[Pending: the robustness retention contrasts are not in the pooled summaries.]**")
  lost <- setdiff(paste(p$key, p$sign), paste(r$key, r$sign))
  gained <- setdiff(r$key, p$key)
  if (!length(lost) && setequal(gained, extra)) return("")
  paste0(" **[Check: without the reprocessed records, primary contrasts no longer credible {",
         paste(lost, collapse = ", "), "}; newly credible {", paste(gained, collapse = ", "),
         "}; the surrounding sentence must be updated.]**")
}
```

When multilingual speakers add a third or later language (L3/Ln), the grammars they
already command shape how its morphosyntax is represented and processed. How that prior knowledge is
recruited is a central question dividing contemporary models of L3
morphosyntactic transfer. Wholesale-transfer accounts hold that a single
previously acquired grammar is selected as the basis for the initial L3 grammar,
whether on typological grounds [the Typological Primacy Model: @rothman2011;
@rothman2015] or because the second language enjoys a privileged cognitive status
[the L2 Status Factor: @bardel2007; @falk2011]. Property-by-property accounts
predict instead that transfer is selective and incremental, with individual
structures transferred (and, where helpful, "enhanced") one at a time as the
learner detects structural similarity. The Linguistic Proximity Model
[@westergaard2017; @westergaard2021; @westergaard2023], the Scalpel Model
[@slabakova2017] and the Cumulative-Enhancement Model [@flynn2004] all take that form.
The wholesale position has recent defenders who raise conceptual and empirical objections
to selective transfer [@schwartzsprouse2021], and initial-stage evidence from early
Catalan--Spanish bilinguals, whose performance on four properties was compatible with
Catalan as the single source of their initial English grammar, has been read as support
for it [@gonzalezalonso2021]. Distinguishing these positions requires more than observing
that prior-language congruence or a miniature language conditions performance. It requires
contrasts for which the accounts make mutually exclusive predictions, measurements early
enough to identify the initial representation before learning can obscure its provenance,
and evidence that distinguishes representational transfer from transient effects of
attention and processing [@gonzalezalonso2020; @gonzalezalonso2025]. Longitudinal
data are essential for characterising development, but later trajectories do not by
themselves recover which representational state initiated that development
[@puigmayenco2025].

## Electrophysiology of morphosyntactic processing

Event-related potentials (ERPs) provide a millisecond-resolution index of how the
brain responds to grammatical violations and are therefore well suited to
characterising when language-conditioned processing diverges, including before a
difference surfaces in overt behaviour. They do not, on their own, establish that a
difference reflects a copied grammatical representation rather than attention, anomaly
detection or another process engaged by the task [@gonzalezalonso2020]. Most evidence on L3 morphosyntactic transfer has come from offline, untimed
acceptability judgements [@puigmayenco2020; @skalba2026]. These index the outcome of
learning. They leave untouched the moment-to-moment processing that ERPs expose
[@angelovska2023; @rothmanalemanbanon2015]. A single-trial ERP design can therefore test
whether prior-language structure covaries with online comprehension. The imbalance is
visible in the literature itself (@fig-literature). In all,
`r lit_n("All L3-transfer research")` records on L3 transfer were indexed between
`r lit_years()`. Of those, `r lit_n("Acceptability/grammaticality judgement")` used
acceptability or grammaticality judgements and `r lit_n("Electrophysiology (ERP/EEG)")`
used electrophysiology, a ratio of roughly `r lit_ratio()` to one. The field has grown
steadily while its electrophysiological base has not. Online evidence has nonetheless
begun to appear. Eye-tracking in early learners of Norwegian shows facilitative and
non-facilitative influence from each prior language on different properties
[@skalba2026].

```{r}
#| label: fig-literature
#| fig-cap: "Methodological Composition of the L3-Transfer Literature Indexed in Scopus, by Publication Year"
#| apa-note: "Each line gives the number of Scopus records per publication year. All records are those matching the L3-transfer query. Judgement tasks and ERP/EEG are the subsets whose title, abstract or keywords also mention acceptability or grammaticality judgements, or event-related potentials, ERP or EEG (electroencephalography). The two subsets can overlap, and none of the three is restricted to morphosyntax. Where the two subsets have the same count, only the ERP/EEG line is visible. The counts index relative composition and are not an exhaustive census: Scopus under-covers books and chapters, keyword matching errs in both directions, and records indexed late may still be added for the most recent years. The retrieval queries are recorded in the project repository."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: !expr if (!is.null(.lit_tbl)) 2.8 else 1
lit_tbl <- .lit_tbl
if (!is.null(lit_tbl)) {
  lt <- lit_tbl
  # Short series names for the direct labels. The CSV strata are left as they are, because
  # lit_n() looks the counts up by them. ERP/EEG is the last level, so it is drawn on top
  # where the two subsets coincide.
  .lit_strata <- c("All L3-transfer research", "Acceptability/grammaticality judgement",
                   "Electrophysiology (ERP/EEG)")
  .lit_series <- c("All records", "Judgement tasks", "ERP/EEG")
  lt$series <- factor(.lit_series[match(lt$stratum, .lit_strata)], levels = .lit_series)
  .y_top <- ceiling(max(lt$n, na.rm = TRUE) / 10) * 10
  # Direct labels at each line's last year. The two subsets end close together, so their
  # labels are kept at least 7% of the y range apart, in the order of their counts.
  lab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(lt, lt$series), function(d) d[which.max(d$year), ]))
  lab$ly <- lab$n
  .gap <- 0.07 * .y_top
  ij <- match(c("Judgement tasks", "ERP/EEG"), lab$series)
  if (!anyNA(ij) && abs(lab$ly[ij[1]] - lab$ly[ij[2]]) < .gap) {
    lo <- max(mean(lab$ly[ij]) - .gap / 2, 0)
    lab$ly[ij] <- if (lab$n[ij[1]] >= lab$n[ij[2]]) c(lo + .gap, lo) else c(lo, lo + .gap)
  }
  ggplot(lt, aes(year, n, colour = series)) +
    les_ref_h(0) +
    geom_line(linewidth = LES_LWD) + geom_point(size = 1.4) +
    geom_text(data = lab, aes(x = year + 0.5, y = ly, label = series), hjust = 0,
              colour = LES_INK, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`All records` = "grey45", `Judgement tasks` = "#CC79A7",
                                   `ERP/EEG` = "#000000"), guide = "none") +
    # The panel ends 0.3 years after the last point, so the labels (0.5 years after it)
    # sit in the margin, where no grid or zero line can run through them. xlim is set on
    # the coord so the label positions do not widen the panel.
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2005, 2025, 5), expand = expansion(add = c(1, 0.3))) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, .y_top, 10), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.04))) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = range(lt$year), ylim = c(0, .y_top), clip = "off") +
    labs(x = "Publication year", y = "Records per year") +
    les_theme(grid = "y") + theme(plot.margin = margin(6, 80, 4, 4))
} else {
  les_placeholder("The literature counts are not yet available.")
}
```
Three components are relevant here. The left-anterior negativity (LAN) is often linked to
automatic morphosyntactic agreement checking. The N400, a negativity sensitive to
lexical--semantic and thematic integration [@frisch2001; @nieuwland2013], also marks the
early stages of morphosyntactic learning, before a late positivity emerges with rising
proficiency [@osterhout2006]. That later positivity is the P600, first reported for words
inconsistent with the preferred syntactic analysis [@osterhout1992]. Over
centro-posterior sites, it has since been associated with syntactic reanalysis and repair,
and with the late integration of syntactic and semantic information
[@friederici2002tics; @friederici2002pnas]. These map onto the three latency windows
analysed here (200--500, 300--600 and 400--900 ms). Training studies show that the brain's response to
second-language violations becomes more native-like as proficiency increases
[@morganshort2012], and again across a consolidation
interval containing no further exposure [@morganshort2012plos], with negativities and
P600s emerging or shifting over time. Native speakers [@tanner2014] and learners
[@tanner2013] also differ systematically from one another in whether they recruit a more
negativity-dominated or a more P600-dominated response. Artificial-language paradigms, in
which the input is fully controlled, have been particularly valuable for isolating
these dynamics from the confounds of natural-language exposure
[@gonzalezalonso2020; @friederici2002pnas]. Bilinguals learning such a language show a
P600 to syntactic violations at a lower proficiency than monolinguals do [@grey2018].

The closest antecedent to the present design is the artificial-language L3 ERP work of
@gonzalezalonso2020. Its findings shape both our predictions and our reading of the
results, so we set them out in full. Fifty first-language-Spanish, second-language-English
bilinguals were given implicit training on one of two miniature languages, built on
English and Spanish lexicons, and their ERPs to gender-agreement violations were recorded
at first exposure. They named their two languages after those lexicons, and we refer to
their groups by lexicon throughout, so that neither is confused with our own Mini-English
and Mini-Norwegian conditions. The two groups responded differently. In their
English-lexicon language, violations elicited an early (200--500 ms) fronto-lateral
negativity, confined to electrodes in the right-anterior region and followed by nothing in
later windows. In their Spanish-lexicon language, they elicited a broadly distributed
positivity at 300--600 ms. Neither group produced a P600 or
any other canonical index of grammatical processing, and judgement accuracy did not differ
between the groups. The authors read the between-group
difference as differential allocation of attention, driven by each miniature language's
lexical similarity to a prior grammar, and therefore as a precursor of source selection,
not as grammatical processing itself. The present study extends that logic in
three ways. It goes beyond first exposure, tracking each property across up to four
sessions, and it manipulates three properties whose relation to the prior grammars
differs within the same learners. It also closes with an unrehearsed retention test
after months without exposure, so the durability of the observed processing effects can be measured.
Whether the initial-exposure pattern of @gonzalezalonso2020 reappears under these
conditions is itself an empirical question, taken up in the Discussion.

Two behavioural studies share more of the present materials. Each trained speakers on a
miniature language with a Norwegian lexicon and a case system, a property Norwegian
lacks. Prior knowledge of a case language eased acquisition even though the lexicon
pointed to Norwegian, but only where that language and the miniature language marked case
in the same overt form, on the noun [@mitrofanova2023; @castle2026]. Greek, which marks
case on the determiner, gave no such advantage in the first study, and the second found
the advantage subject to word-order bias and proficiency. The overt realisation of a
property conditioned crosslinguistic influence, and the present gender manipulation varies exactly
that realisation between the two miniature languages.

Recent syntheses of the transfer
literature draw attention to the methodological choices that constrain what its findings
can show [@puigmayenco2020; @rothman2019; @gonzalezalonso2026], and longitudinal and
electrophysiological evidence remains among its scarcest. An ERP successor to
@gonzalezalonso2020 trained heritage and second-language bilinguals on a Latin
mini-grammar and found violation responses that no current model had predicted, an
outcome its authors took as a question about the paradigm itself [@pereirasoares2022].
The recurring objection to miniature languages is that a
grammar acquired in hours may not engage the mechanisms of natural morphosyntax. This
literature answers it with the finding that artificial-language learners, once
sufficiently proficient, show qualitatively native-like violation responses
[@morganshort2012; @friederici2002pnas]. What the design buys in exchange is exact
control over every learner's input history, which no natural-language design can offer.

## The present study

We use a controlled artificial-language design to ask whether learners' sensitivity to
three morphosyntactic properties, in judgements and in the ERP response, differs between
two miniature languages, and how that sensitivity develops from the first post-training
session to a retention test months later. Norwegian--English bilinguals (first language
Norwegian, second language English) acquired one of two miniature languages, Mini-English
or Mini-Norwegian. Within each language, we manipulated three morphosyntactic properties
that vary in their relationship to the learners' existing grammars: subject--verb gender
agreement, differential object marking and verb--object number agreement. The two languages
share their grammatical morphemes and differ in two respects. Their content words are built
on English and on Norwegian stems respectively, and gender is marked by a free prenominal
determiner in Mini-English but by a determiner suffixed to the noun in Mini-Norwegian, as the
Norwegian definite article is (see Method).

Single-trial ERPs and grammaticality judgements were collected across four
laboratory sessions (Sessions 2, 3, 4 and 6) that trace the learning trajectory
from the first post-training session to a post-consolidation retention test. The properties
enter the design at different points (gender agreement from Session 2,
differential object marking from Session 3 and verb--object number agreement from
Session 4), yielding a cumulative, property-by-property exposure schedule (@fig-design).

```{r}
#| label: fig-design
#| fig-cap: "Exposure and Measurement Schedule"
#| apa-note: "Points mark the sessions at which each grammatical property was presented and tested. Each property enters at a different session and recurs at every later one, so gender agreement is tested at four sessions, differential object marking at three and verb--object number agreement at two. Sessions 1 and 5 were home sessions of the cognitive battery analysed in a companion paper, and Session 1 also included the Language History Questionnaire. Neither session included training or testing in the miniature language, so both are omitted. The session axis is ordinal, and equal spacing does not imply equal elapsed time. The brackets above the grid give the intervals: Sessions 2 to 4 were one week apart, and Session 6, the unrehearsed retention test, followed Session 4 after about four months without exposure."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 2.0
.props <- unname(LES_PROPERTY_LABELS_FIG)
# Each property's first tested session, in the order of LES_PROPERTY_LABELS_FIG; the
# sessions themselves come from the data manifest.
.entry <- c(2, 3, 4)
.sess  <- LES_ERP_SESSIONS
stopifnot(length(.entry) == length(.props), all(.entry %in% .sess))
# Only the tested cells are drawn: a property is absent by design before it enters.
design <- expand.grid(s = .sess, p = seq_along(.props))
design <- design[design$s >= .entry[design$p], ]
design$x <- match(design$s, .sess)
design$Property <- factor(.props[design$p], levels = rev(.props))   # gender at the top
# The session axis is deliberately ORDINAL, not metric: it encodes which property was
# tested when, and makes no claim about elapsed time. The intervals between sessions are
# very unequal (one week between Sessions 2-4, about four months before Session 6), so
# they are given in brackets above the grid. A metric axis would also invite a false
# reading, since attrition over the retention interval is heavy (see @fig-flow).
.top <- length(.props) + 0.2    # top of the dot grid, where the session guides stop
.by  <- length(.props) + 0.62   # bracket height, above the grid
# The session guides are segments that stop at the top of the grid. A theme grid would
# span the whole panel, which the brackets extend, and so run up through the bracket
# ticks. The segments take the house grid's colour and width.
.guide <- calc_element("panel.grid.major.x", les_theme(grid = "x"))
ggplot(design, aes(x = x, y = Property)) +
  annotate("segment", x = seq_along(.sess), xend = seq_along(.sess), y = -Inf, yend = .top,
           colour = .guide$colour, linewidth = .guide$linewidth) +
  geom_point(size = 3.4, colour = LES_INK) +
  annotate("segment", x = 1:3 + 0.03, xend = 2:4 - 0.03, y = .by, yend = .by,
           colour = "grey45", linewidth = 0.35) +
  # One tick at each session, shared by the two brackets that meet there.
  annotate("segment", x = seq_along(.sess), xend = seq_along(.sess),
           y = .by - 0.07, yend = .by + 0.07, colour = "grey45", linewidth = 0.35) +
  annotate("text", x = c(1.5, 2.5, 3.5), y = .by + 0.17, vjust = 0, colour = "grey20",
           size = LES_TEXT_PT / .pt,
           label = c("1 week", "1 week", "≈ 4 months, no exposure")) +
  # A narrow x expansion widens the session steps, so the Session 4-6 label keeps clear
  # of the ticks at either end of its bracket.
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq_along(.sess), labels = .sess,
                     expand = expansion(add = 0.15)) +
  scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.45, 0.2))) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "Session", y = NULL) +
  les_theme(grid = "none") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey10"), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        plot.margin = margin(24, 8, 4, 4))
```

The transfer accounts make their clearest predictions for gender agreement, the only one of
the three properties that Norwegian has and English lacks. The Typological Primacy Model
holds that the parser selects a whole prior grammar on the basis of overall similarity,
assessed from a hierarchy of cues in which the lexicon comes first [@rothman2015]. A
Mini-Norwegian learner should therefore draw on Norwegian, gender included, and a
Mini-English learner on English, which has no grammatical gender. The model predicts greater
sensitivity to gender-agreement violations in the Mini-Norwegian group, in the judgements
and in the ERP response, at least at the earliest sessions, before further input could
overcome a non-facilitative choice. This is the prediction that
@rothmanalemanbanon2015 derived for the analogous Mini-Spanish and Mini-English groups. The
L2 Status Factor predicts instead that both groups draw on English [@bardel2007;
@falk2011], so that neither gains an advantage from Norwegian gender. Property-by-property
accounts make no such prediction from grammatical knowledge alone. The Norwegian gender
system remains available to every participant, and a learner of either miniature language
can recruit it once the input reveals that the property is shared [@westergaard2017;
@westergaard2021]. On that derivation, the two groups need not differ.

Two features of the design limit what a group difference could show. First, the Linguistic
Proximity Model allows superficial, especially lexical, similarity to sway influence at the
earliest stages, before learners can detect abstract structural similarity
[@westergaard2017; @westergaard2021]. A Mini-Norwegian advantage would therefore not refute
property-by-property transfer, a point made both about artificial-language evidence of this
kind [@jensen2023] and about the closest ERP precedent [@gonzalezalonso2020]. Second, the two
miniature languages differ in structure as well as in lexicon, because Mini-Norwegian marks
gender on a suffixed determiner, as Norwegian does. Structural similarity of that kind is
what property-by-property accounts take to trigger selective transfer, so they too could
expect Mini-Norwegian learners to recruit Norwegian gender more readily. A Mini-Norwegian
advantage in gender-agreement sensitivity is therefore compatible with every account except
the L2 Status Factor. The accounts separate on its absence, which the Typological Primacy
Model does not allow and property-by-property accounts do. Differential object marking and
verb--object number agreement are absent from both prior languages and realised identically
in the two miniature languages, so no account predicts a group difference in sensitivity to
either. They serve as controls for group differences that arise for reasons other than the
prior grammars, such as a difference in how easily the two lexicons are learned.

These predictions concern the source of grammatical knowledge, but the measures record
processing and decisions. A judgement also reflects how readily a learner accepts sentences
at all, and a violation response can reflect attention or anomaly detection as well as
grammatical computation [@gonzalezalonso2020]. We therefore separate sensitivity to
grammaticality from the criterion applied in the judgement, using signal detection theory
[@macmillan2005; @huang2020], and read a group difference in sensitivity as the stronger
evidence about grammatical knowledge in this design. The development of sensitivity across
sessions, and its change over the retention interval, are characterised for each property.
The transfer accounts make no distinct prediction about retention, for which the expectation
comes from training studies in which a grammaticality response that emerged during training
holds or grows across months without exposure [@morganshort2012plos]. Because the first
measurement follows training, no observation here captures an initial state free of learning
[@gonzalezalonso2017; @gonzalezalonso2025].

Alongside the region-averaged models, we ask whether grammaticality is decodable from the
whole-scalp voltage pattern at each moment. A multivariate decoder can detect a
distributed violation response too weak to move any single region's mean. Its
cross-language generalisation asks whether the pattern that separates the conditions in
one mini-language also separates them in the other. Its cross-property generalisation
tests a further prediction. If the grammaticality response were largely a domain-general
salience or integration signal [@sassenhagen2019; @aurnhammer2023], a decoder trained on
one property should transfer to the others. If each property recruits its own code, as
the fractionation of the late positivity [@kaan2003] and the separable developmental
courses of agreement features [@alemanbanon2018] suggest, it should not. No null
distribution was computed for either generalisation analysis, so both are reported as
descriptive probes.

# Method

## Participants

In total, `r flow_n("enrolled")` Norwegian--English bilinguals (first
language Norwegian, second language English) took part, each assigned to learn one
of the two miniature languages. At the Norwegian site, odd-numbered participant
identifiers were assigned to Mini-English and even-numbered identifiers to
Mini-Norwegian, a deterministic allocation and not a random one. That rule gave
`r flow_n("enrolled", "n_mini_english")` Mini-English and
`r flow_n("enrolled", "n_mini_norwegian")` Mini-Norwegian learners, so language is a
between-participants factor.`r abstract_guard()`
The six-session protocol comprised an approximately 1.5-hour home baseline (Session 1),
laboratory sessions of approximately 2.5 hours (Session 2), 2.5 hours (Session 3), and
3 hours (Session 4), a 1-hour home retest (Session 5), and a 2.5-hour laboratory
retention session (Session 6). Of the `r pstat("n_lhq3", "value", 0)` participants
with a Language History Questionnaire record [LHQ3: @lhq3], the mean age was
`r pstat("age_years")` years ($SD = `r pstat("age_years", "sd")`$, range
`r pstat("age_years", "vmin", 0)`--`r pstat("age_years", "vmax", 0)`).`r minors_note()`
Of the same record, `r pstat("sex_female", "value", 0)` identified as female,
`r pstat("sex_male", "value", 0)` as male and `r pstat("sex_nonbinary", "value", 0)`
as non-binary (`r pstat("sex_undisclosed", "value", 0)` did not disclose). Among the
`r pstat("hand_reported_n", "value", 0)` who reported handedness,
`r pstat("hand_right", "value", 0)` were right-handed and
`r pstat("hand_left", "value", 0)` left-handed. English had been
acquired early (age of first exposure $M = `r pstat("eng_aoa_listen")`$ years,
$SD = `r pstat("eng_aoa_listen", "sd")`$) and used for many years
($M = `r pstat("eng_years")`$, $SD = `r pstat("eng_years", "sd")`$), with high
self-rated proficiency ($M = `r pstat("eng_l2_proficiency", "value", 2)`$ of 1,
$SD = `r pstat("eng_l2_proficiency", "sd", 2)`$). `r other_lang_sentence()`

Attrition increased across the training: of the `r flow_n("enrolled")` who began,
`r flow_n("attended_S3")` remained at Session 3, `r flow_n("attended_S4")` at
Session 4, and `r flow_n("attended_S6")` completed the Session 6 retention test.
One participant assigned to Mini-Norwegian is excluded from every analysis, although they
are counted among those enrolled and attending. At Session 2, the laboratory computer ran
the other study site's experiment file, which assigned that participant's identifier to
Mini-English, so they were trained and tested in Mini-English at that session and in
Mini-Norwegian from Session 3 onwards. The presentation log and the EEG trigger record agree
on what was shown, so the error lies in what was presented, not in how it was recorded.
Because the lexicon and the first property are trained at Session 2, this participant's
trajectory belongs to neither group. The exclusion rests on that design argument and not on
this participant's results, which were not examined separately.
The ERP analyses draw on the `r flow_n("usable_erp")` participants with usable
single-trial EEG (`r flow_n("usable_erp", "n_mini_english")` Mini-English,
`r flow_n("usable_erp", "n_mini_norwegian")` Mini-Norwegian). The fitted ERP models
also require the L1-dominance covariate described under *Data analysis*, and the trials
of a participant without that score are dropped by listwise deletion, so the
gender-agreement models were fitted to `r erp_model_n("gender_agreement")`
participants, the differential-object-marking models to
`r erp_model_n("differential_object_marking")` and the verb--object number-agreement
models to `r erp_model_n("verb_object_number_agreement")`. The
grammaticality-judgement analyses draw on `r flow_n("usable_accuracy")` participants
(@fig-flow).

The project was registered with the Norwegian Agency for Shared Services in
Education and Research (Sikt; project 2559611). *[The approving ethics committee, approval date and reference number are to be supplied.]* All procedures complied
with the relevant laws and institutional guidelines, the privacy rights of the participants
were observed, and every participant gave written informed consent. The 16-year-old
participant was covered by the study's self-consent procedure. Participants were
compensated with shopping vouchers worth NOK 250 per hour of participation, pro rata,
and received an additional NOK 400 completion bonus after the sixth and final session.

```{r}

      n_b = c(g("usable_accuracy", "n_mini_english"), g("usable_erp", "n_mini_english"))),
    headings = c("Enrolment and group assignment", "Attendance",

    base_size = LES_FIG_BASE_SIZE)
}
```

## Design and materials

The longitudinal artificial-language paradigm and the participants are those of the
project reported by @gonzalezalonso2025, restricted to its Norwegian site, so that
project's Spanish site is not included here. Within each language, the design crosses
grammaticality (contrast coded
grammatical $= +0.5$, ungrammatical $= -0.5$) with session (the cumulative exposure
schedule above) within participants, and language between participants
(Mini-Norwegian $= +0.5$, Mini-English $= -0.5$), so a positive language-bearing
coefficient indicates a larger value for the Mini-Norwegian group. The three
properties were analysed separately. Each was probed with 48 grammatical and 48
ungrammatical sentences per session, built from a closed lexicon of twelve nouns, twelve
adjectives, twelve transitive verbs and twelve proper names per language. A third,
ancillary violation type was recorded but is not analysed here. Each sentence frame was
presented in both a grammatical and an ungrammatical version. The two miniature
languages draw on separate content lexicons, Mini-English building its nouns,
adjectives, verbs and names on English stems and Mini-Norwegian on
Norwegian stems. The critical word
carried the EEG trigger that defined the single-trial time-lock.

The two miniature languages share the same invented grammatical morphemes (the
determiners *je*/*ze*/*jer*/*zer*, the object marker *fi*, the verbal suffix *-evo*
and the adjectival agreement suffixes). They differ in one structural dimension,
determiner position, and that difference is the pivot of the transfer contrast.
Subject--verb gender agreement is built on a two-way common/neuter distinction, as
in real Norwegian. Each noun carries the gender of its Norwegian translation equivalent,
and the same noun carries the same gender in both miniature languages, so gender assignment
never conflicts with Norwegian and the two languages differ in where gender is marked and
not in which gender a noun takes. In Mini-English, the determiner is a free prenominal word that
marks gender and number (*je*/*ze* for common/neuter singular, *jer*/*zer* for
the plural), as English articles are free-standing. In Mini-Norwegian, the same
gender--number determiner is a bound suffix on the noun (e.g. *gateje*/*gatejer*),
as the Norwegian definite article is suffixal. In both languages, the predicate
adjective carries a matching agreement suffix, on which the gender-agreement
violation is realised. Differential object marking is a free particle *fi* placed
before the object noun phrase, identical in the two languages, with the violation
omitting it. Verb--object number agreement is a verbal suffix *-evo* that marks the
verb to agree with a plural object, again identical across languages, with the
violation a number mismatch between verb and object.

These three properties map onto the learners' existing grammars differently, which
is what the language factor exploits. Grammatical gender expressed through a
suffixed determiner is a property of the learners' first language, Norwegian, but
not of their second language, English. The Mini-Norwegian realisation therefore
aligns closely with the first-language grammar, whereas the Mini-English realisation expresses
a feature that English does not encode (gender) through an English-like free
determiner. Differential object marking and verb--object number agreement, by
contrast, are absent from both Norwegian and English, so neither is supported by a
prior grammar in either group.

## Procedure

Sentences were presented one word at a time in the centre of the screen (rapid serial
visual presentation, RSVP) using OpenSesame 3.3.14. Word duration was a deterministic
function of word length. A non-critical word was shown for
$250 + 35 \times (\text{characters} - 3)$ ms, floored at 250 ms, giving durations of
250--600 ms. The critical word was shown for 40 ms less than a non-critical word of the
same length (210--560 ms). Non-critical words followed one another at a stimulus-onset
asynchrony of approximately 505 ms. At the critical word, the asynchrony was held
fixed at approximately 750 ms, with the following blank interval lengthened to compensate for
the varying word duration. The timing of the post-critical region therefore did not depend
on the length of the critical word. The critical word occupied the third or fourth position and
was followed by three to six further words. Presentation was entirely
experimenter-paced. Nothing in the sentence stream depended on the participant, so a
condition difference in reading speed cannot shift the epoch. The grammaticality judgement
was requested only after the final word of the sentence, never during it, and was made with
a two-button response (left = grammatical, right = violation). No motor response therefore
fell inside the analysed epoch. Participants were instructed to minimise movement and
blinking, especially during the presentation of words. During pauses in these long
sessions, experimenters monitored the signal and intervened when necessary to maintain
low electrode impedance and acceptable signal quality.

This timing has one consequence for the late window. The raw presentation logs record
all `r rsvp_tim("n_trials", big = TRUE)` critical-word trials, a census taken before any
EEG-side exclusion, so its count exceeds the modelled trial numbers. In that census,
exactly one subsequent word onset falls within 900 ms
of the critical word (the per-trial maximum is
`r rsvp_tim("max_onsets_within_900ms")`), at `r rsvp_tim("next_onset_min_ms")`--`r rsvp_tim("next_onset_max_ms")` ms
(median `r rsvp_tim("next_onset_median_ms")` ms).`r rsvp_one_guard()` The final roughly 150 ms of the
400--900 ms measurement window therefore contains the beginning of the response to the
following word. This is unavoidable in connected-sentence RSVP at this rate, and it is
constant across conditions because the post-critical asynchrony is held fixed, so it cannot
manufacture a grammaticality effect. Late-window amplitudes should nonetheless be read as
containing that overlap, not as a pure response to the critical word.

## EEG acquisition and single-trial ERP quantification

Continuous EEG was recorded with a 32-channel Brain Products LiveAmp system, using active
electrodes in an extended 10--20 layout with the CACS-32 cap montage recorded in the data
headers. The sampling rate was 500 Hz and the online passband DC--131 Hz, with no online
notch filter. The 131 Hz anti-aliasing low-pass is a causal acquisition filter, so it
imposes no phase distortion of the kind that motivates the offline filter choices set out
below.

Three channel counts appear in what follows, and they refer to different things, so we
set them out once. Thirty-two electrodes were recorded. Two of them, TP9 and TP10, become
the offline linked-mastoid reference and are therefore not analysed as signals. FCz served
as the online reference and is recovered as a channel when the data are re-referenced. The
remaining 30 electrodes are the ones assigned to the nine analysis regions, so they are
what the region-averaged amplitude models use and the electrodes from which the scalp maps are estimated.
The decoder ignores the region map and takes every EEG channel available in
all contributing sessions, which is those 30 plus the recovered FCz, giving 31 features.
The LiveAmp's three accelerometer traces (`x_dir`, `y_dir`, `z_dir`) are movement signals,
not brain signals, and are excluded throughout. The Session 2 exports additionally retain
TP9, TP10 and the accelerometer channels, whereas the Session 3, 4 and 6 exports do not,
which is why the decoder uses only the channels common to every session. Offline, in
BrainVision Analyzer, the data were re-referenced to the mean of the two mastoids, with FCz
recovered, and then band-pass filtered with zero-phase-shift (forward and reverse)
Butterworth IIR filters, high-pass 0.1 Hz and low-pass 30 Hz, each specified in Analyzer as
fourth order. Analyzer realises that specification as a second-order filter applied
forwards and then backwards, so the combined zero-phase response is the fourth-order one,
falling off at 24 dB per octave. A scripted reconstruction of the processing chain
reproduced Analyzer's exported data to the precision of the export only under that
reading. No notch filter was applied
offline. Filtering preceded ocular correction, so the independent component analysis was
trained on the same 0.1 Hz high-passed data that the analyses themselves use. It was
computed on each whole recording, leaving out intervals marked as bad during raw-data
inspection, and components were selected semi-automatically. In Sessions 3, 4 and 6, TP9 and
TP10 had been discarded at re-referencing, so the decomposition used the 30 remaining
electrodes (29 in one Session 3 recording in which CP2 had been interpolated). In Session 2
it used 32 electrodes, the 30 scalp electrodes and TP9 and TP10. The recovered FCz passed
through it unchanged in every session.

In Session 2, the re-referencing step also included the online reference in the average,
so those recordings were exported against the mean of TP9, TP10 and a zero-valued FCz
instead of against the mean of the mastoids, and TP9 and TP10 were kept. We brought them to
the reference of the other sessions offline, as each export was read. Subtracting a sixth of
the sum of the exported TP9 and TP10 from each scalp electrode re-references the ocularly
corrected scalp data to the ocularly corrected mastoids, an identity that holds on the
exports to their precision. FCz bypassed the ocular correction, so 1.5 times its exported
value is the linked-mastoid FCz exactly. Against a linked-mastoid branch that the
analyst had built, but not exported, in one participant's Session 2 history, the correction
was four times more accurate than a simpler alternative that adds half of the exported FCz
to every channel. That alternative is exact before ocular correction but not after it, and
it was applied in an earlier version of these analyses. Without any correction, the Session 2
grammaticality effects in four recordings rebuilt from the raw data would have been
displaced by up to 2.3 µV relative to the other sessions.

Owing to a processing oversight, the Session 3 recordings of nine participants were
high-pass filtered at 1 Hz rather than 0.1 Hz. The archived Analyzer histories show a single
1 Hz filter node from which their exports descend, and a scripted rebuild of those exports
from the raw recordings reproduces them only at 1 Hz. A 1 Hz high-pass is a documented
generator of artefacts in this kind of paradigm [@tanner2015; @widmann2015], so the 1 Hz
data enter no analysis. The nine recordings were instead reprocessed from the raw data under a
protocol fixed before any reprocessed output was inspected. A scripted reconstruction of the
archived processing first reproduced every one of their 1 Hz exports to within the rounding
of the export (root-mean-square error below 0.0004 µV), and only then was the high-pass
cutoff changed to 0.1 Hz, with every other step and every retained trial kept as archived.
The reprocessed data enter every fitted ERP model, the decoding and the ERP
displays.`r misfilter_status()` A robustness analysis fixed in the same protocol refits the
ERP models and the confirmatory decoding without them. It can qualify a primary result but
not create one. The decision rests on the filter setting itself and on nothing observed in
these participants' data, so it is not results-contingent. The argument is set out in
@apx-analytic-decisions-in-detail. `r misfilter_share_sentence()`

Every exported trial was then traced to its source recording through the export's time
stamps and the processing history, and every export was checked for a stimulus-locked
response. Three exports failed, and each failure was confirmed on the EEG itself. The
Session 3 export of one participant is a second copy of another participant's Session 3
recording. The Session 6 export of a second participant was segmented at the event times of
that participant's Session 4 recording, and the Session 2 export of a third participant at
the event times of a recording other than the one archived. The epochs of the last two are
not time-locked to any stimulus and show no evoked response. None of the three exports
measures the participant-session it is named for. The same protocol allows a misaligned
record to be recovered only if its archived processing decisions were made on the
participant's own recording, which it tests by first reproducing the legacy export from that
recording. The two misaligned records passed: each export was reproduced from the
participant's own archived recording and the event markers its processing history carries,
to the same precision as the filter reconstruction, so only the event markers had come from
another recording. Each record was then re-segmented at its own events by the trigger rule
described below, inside the stretch of recording the analyst had processed and inspected,
with every epoch that overlaps a marked bad interval dropped and no manual epoch removal
carried over. The recovered records enter the primary analysis, and the robustness analysis
drops them together with the nine reprocessed ones. The duplicated Session 3 export cannot be
recovered, because none of its processing decisions was made on that participant's
recording, so it is excluded from every EEG analysis. The accuracy models retain all of these
sessions, because neither the filter nor the segmentation bears on the judgement logs.

Each critical word was marked by four serial-port triggers sent in succession as the word
was drawn: the word identity, which marks word onset, then the sentence identity, the
grammatical property and the grammaticality condition. After ocular correction, each record
was segmented in two steps. The first step cut 1,200 ms epochs beginning 120 ms before the
property trigger, and these were screened semi-automatically: epochs containing a voltage
step above 30 µV/ms, a range above 100 µV within 200 ms or activity below 0.5 µV within
100 ms were flagged, and the operator reviewed the flagged epochs, removing some and keeping
most. The second step cut 1,200 ms epochs beginning 130 ms before the condition trigger, and
kept an epoch only if it lay wholly within a retained first-step epoch. That holds only when
the condition trigger fell exactly five samples after the property trigger. The triggers had
a nominal spacing of 10 ms, but the realised spacing averaged about 10.7 ms, so at 500 Hz
the two triggers were six samples apart for about a third of critical words, and those
words yielded no epoch. An audit of the behavioural logs, marker files, processing histories
and exports of every participant-session traced each loss to its cause: in the processing
histories, `r aud("events_history_lag_not5")` of the `r aud("events_history")` critical-word
events had an interval other than five samples, and none of them reached an export, whereas
`r aud("epochs_removed")` first-step epochs were removed on review, every one of them flagged
by the criteria (`r aud("epochs_flagged")` were flagged in all). The share of words kept by
the trigger rule ranged from `r aud("lag5_share_recording_min")`% to
`r aud("lag5_share_recording_max")`% across recordings, mainly with how quickly the stimulus
computer sent the triggers. Within recordings, loss was unrelated to grammaticality (odds of
losing an ungrammatical rather than a grammatical trial
`r aud("or_loss_ungrammatical_vs_grammatical", 2)`,
`r aud_ci("or_loss_ungrammatical_vs_grammatical")`), response accuracy and item, and only
weakly and inconsistently related to response time and trial position, so it lowers
precision without favouring either side of the grammaticality contrast. It was not
perfectly even across groups and sessions, however. The largest imbalance was in the
Mini-English group at Session 6, where grammatical retention fell below ungrammatical
retention for every property, by `r aud("s6_me_gap_gender_pp", 1, abs = TRUE)`,
`r aud("s6_me_gap_dom_pp", 1, abs = TRUE)` and `r aud("s6_me_gap_voa_pp", 1, abs = TRUE)`
percentage points of the 48 presented trials for gender agreement, differential object
marking and verb--object number agreement, and by `r aud("s6_me_gap_mean_pp", 1, abs = TRUE)`
points on average (odds ratio `r aud("s6_me_or_loss_ungrammatical_vs_grammatical", 2)`,
`r aud_ci("s6_me_or_loss_ungrammatical_vs_grammatical")`). A segmentation tolerant of one
sample of trigger jitter would have kept `r aud("tolerant_trials_ratio", 1)` times as many
trials, but projected onto the trial-level structure of the ERP models it would have narrowed
the interval of the gender-agreement grammaticality $\times$ language term by only
`r aud("gl_narrowing_trialdep_pct_min")`--`r aud("gl_narrowing_trialdep_pct_max")`%, so the
recordings were not re-exported. Differential trial loss between the compared conditions would make a
grammaticality effect partly a difference in measurement precision and only partly one in
brain response, so retention is reported per condition. On average, `r erp_ret("mean")` of the 48 presented
trials were retained per modelled cell ($SD = `r erp_ret("sd")`$), so
`r erp_ret("pct_discarded")`% were not retained. These retention figures are counted from the
single-trial data the models were fitted to, after every exclusion and with the reprocessed
and recovered records as analysed. @tbl-retention-trials gives the full per-condition
breakdown, averaged over the two groups. Averaged over properties and sessions as well, a
participant retained `r ret_by_gram("Grammatical")` of the 48 grammatical trials and
`r ret_by_gram("Ungrammatical")` of the 48 ungrammatical ones, a difference of
`r ret_gram_gap()` trials. Epoch time is labelled from $-100$ to $1098$ ms relative
to word onset on the assumption of the nominal trigger spacing; relative to the recorded
word-identity trigger, the labels understate elapsed time by
`r aud("label_offset_mean_ms", 1)` ms on average and by at most
`r aud("label_offset_max_ms")` ms, which is negligible for window mean amplitudes. The audit's
scripts and the tables these figures are read from are in the project repository
(`paper_1_transfer/audit/`).

The observed elapsed duration of each home task and of each phase of the laboratory
sessions is shown in @fig-home-task-duration and @fig-lab-phase-duration. These are
descriptive timing checks, not additional outcomes: home-task duration runs from the
first to the last Gorilla event for each participant and task, whereas lab-phase duration
uses the OpenSesame phase markers and the final event in a phase when the next phase was
recorded in a separate export.
`r les_task_duration_median_text(task_duration_home, task_duration_lab)`

```{r}
#| label: fig-home-task-duration
#| fig-cap: "Duration of the Home Cognitive Tasks by Session"
#| apa-note: "Points are participants, and each box summarises their durations for one task and session: the thick line is the median, the box spans the interquartile range, and the whiskers reach the most extreme duration within 1.5 times the interquartile range of the box, computed on the logarithmic scale of the vertical axis. Duration is the elapsed time from the first to the last raw Gorilla event, so it includes instructions, practice and test material when those events are present in the export. Session 1 is the baseline and Session 5 the post-training session. Durations longer than 100 min, each produced by a multi-hour idle gap in the export, lie beyond the top of the axis; a triangle marks them, with their number beside it, and they are included in the box statistics. Participants without a linked enrolled-participant key are excluded. ASRT = alternating serial reaction time."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 2.6
les_task_duration_home_plot(task_duration_home, base_size = LES_FIG_BASE_SIZE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-lab-phase-duration
#| fig-cap: "Duration of the Laboratory-Session Phases"
#| apa-note: "Points are participants, and each box summarises their durations for one phase and session: the thick line is the median, the box spans the interquartile range, and the whiskers reach the most extreme duration within 1.5 times the interquartile range of the box, computed on the logarithmic scale of the vertical axis. A phase runs from its recorded start marker to the next phase's start marker or, when the next phase was exported separately, to the last event of the phase. Pretraining was not recorded at Session 4, and only the experiment phase was recorded at Session 6, so those sessions are absent from the other panels. Sessions 2, 3 and 4 are training sessions, one week apart, and Session 6 is the retention session, about four months after Session 4 without exposure. Sessions are equally spaced on the horizontal axis, which is therefore not proportional to elapsed time."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 2.6
les_task_duration_lab_plot(task_duration_lab, base_size = LES_FIG_BASE_SIZE)
```

For each retained trial, we computed the mean amplitude in three theoretically
motivated latency windows, 200--500 ms (the LAN/early-negativity range),
300--600 ms (the N400 range) and 400--900 ms (the P600 range), at lateral and
midline electrode macroregions. The windows are named by their nominal bounds
throughout. On the 2 ms acquisition grid, each is inclusive of samples up to
`r win_upper_bounds()` ms respectively. That convention follows the validated import procedure
and is noted here so that the figures and the deposited code can be read against the prose. The lateral
region comprises six clusters, left- and right-hemisphere anterior, medial and posterior. The
midline region comprises three clusters centred on the midline. Those clusters are
parasagittal, so they are not strictly midline. Besides Fz, Cz, Pz and Oz they include the pairs
FC1/FC2 and CP1/CP2, which the cap places about a quarter of the head radius either
side of it. Because each pair is exactly symmetric, however, the cluster mean remains
centred on the midline and has no net hemispheric bias. Each trial's amplitude in a
macroregion is the mean over its clusters, each cluster weighted equally whatever its
number of electrodes, so every trial contributes one observation per macroregion. Two further choices, the within-participant $z$-scoring of
single-trial amplitudes and the treatment of each trial's pre-stimulus mean amplitude
($-100$ to $0$ ms) as a covariate instead of a subtracted baseline, are modelling
decisions and are set out under *Data analysis*.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-retention-trials
#| tbl-cap: "Mean Number of EEG Trials Retained per Participant and Condition, by Grammatical Property and Session"
#| apa-note: "Values are means over participants of the trials retained out of the 48 presented per condition, averaged over the two language groups. Rows are split by grammaticality because differential trial loss across the compared conditions can bias both amplitude and decodability. The two conditions are retained almost equally here (see text). A blank cell marks a session at which the property had not yet been introduced. The counts are those of the single-trial data the models were fitted to."
#| apa-longtable: true
if (!is.null(erp_ret_tbl) && has_knitr && "scope" %in% names(erp_ret_tbl)) {
  pc <- erp_ret_tbl[erp_ret_tbl$scope == "per_condition_canonical", , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(pc)) {
    # Factor (not character) so rows follow the order in which the properties were
    # introduced across sessions, rather than alphabetically.
    pc$Property <- factor(.table_props[match(pc$grammatical_property, names(.table_props))],
                          levels = unname(.table_props))
    # Retain grammaticality: averaging over it would remove the very comparison this
    # table exists to license, since differential trial loss between the compared
    # conditions would mean the grammaticality effect is partly a difference in
    # measurement precision rather than in brain response.
    pc$Condition <- factor(pc$grammaticality, levels = c("Grammatical", "Ungrammatical"))
    agg <- aggregate(mean_retained ~ Property + Condition + session, data = pc, FUN = mean)
    agg <- agg[order(agg$Property, agg$Condition), ]
    sess <- sort(unique(agg$session))
    key  <- unique(agg[, c("Property", "Condition")])
    body <- data.frame(Condition = as.character(key$Condition), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    # A session at which the property had not yet entered the design has no row in the
    # aggregate. Such a cell is not applicable by design, so it is left blank (NA prints
    # as an empty cell), which the note explains; an em dash would mean a value that was
    # expected but not obtained.
    for (s in sess) body[[as.character(s)]] <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(key)), function(i) {
      v <- agg$mean_retained[agg$Property == key$Property[i] &
                               agg$Condition == key$Condition[i] & agg$session == s]
      if (length(v) == 1L) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 1) else NA_character_
    }, "")
    les_grid_table(body, header = c("Condition", as.character(sess)),
                   align = c("l", rep("r", length(sess))),
                   spanners = list(list(label = "Session", cols = seq_along(sess) + 1L)),
                   group = .les_group(as.character(key$Property)),
                   decimals = as.character(sess))
  } else knitr::asis_output("*Per-condition retention pending.*")
} else {
  knitr::asis_output("*The per-condition retention table will appear once the trial-retention summary is present.*")
}
```

## Grammaticality-judgement task

The grammaticality judgement was collected concurrently with the ERP recording. On
each experimental trial, participants judged whether the sentence was grammatical for
the property under test, so the trial-level accuracy (correct/incorrect) and the
single-trial ERP are two measures of the same event. The scored judgement is the sole behavioural measure, and it is analysed as
sensitivity and criterion (see *Data analysis*). Rows that the presentation software
logged twice under one trial number (`r rt_screen("n_duplicates_removed")`, each a
re-logging of a file's last trial when the session closed) were first reduced to one per
participant, session, property and trial. Every judgement was then analysed except the
`r rt_dropped_phrase()` without a recorded response time, leaving `r rt_screen("n_kept")`
trials.`r acc_rt_switch_marker()` `r acc_gap_sentence()` `r rt_legacy_sentence()` The
unlabelled filler sentences shown at Session 2 carry no property and fall outside the
modelled contrast. Every judgement sentence filled one of the sentence frames of its
property, which the presentation software marked with the same trigger code in the EEG,
so the judgement trials share the ERP models' item factor (see *Data analysis*).

## Data analysis

All models were fitted in a fully Bayesian framework with `brms` [@burkner2017;
@burkner2018] as a front end to the Stan No-U-Turn sampler [@carpenter2017]. A Bayesian
treatment is not incidental to the question here. The hypotheses concern the size and
direction of effects that are expected to be small. Several of the comparisons that
matter, such as whether a property's language-conditioned effect grows across sessions, are naturally
expressed as statements about a posterior. Priors, sampler settings, diagnostics and
inference rules are set out in the sections that follow.

The analysis and reporting code
was written with the assistance of Claude Code (version 2.1, Anthropic), running
primarily the Claude Opus and Claude Fable models, which drafted and revised scripts
under the authors' direction and checked them against the method reported here. The
authors reviewed and ran every script, and the deposited code reproduces the analyses
without the tool.

### Predictor coding and standardisation

Every continuous predictor was $z$-standardised and every dichotomous predictor
was $\pm 0.5$ contrast coded before model fitting (the $\pm 0.5$ codes are then
$z$-standardised with the other predictors, which preserves their sign). On this
common standardised scale, regression coefficients are directly comparable, and
lower-order terms in interactive models retain interpretable main-effect meanings
[@brauer2018; @schielzeth2010]. Standardising the inputs is also what makes a prior
on a coefficient interpretable, because it fixes the scale that prior is placed on
[@gelman2008]. Session was recoded to consecutive integers in the order the four
sessions occurred, Sessions 2, 3, 4 and 6 becoming 0--3, and then $z$-standardised
(within property for the accuracy models, whose properties span different session
ranges). The change in an effect between any two measured sessions,
including across the retention interval, is then a single linear combination of the
posterior draws. Besides grammaticality (grammatical $= +0.5$) and language
(Mini-Norwegian $= +0.5$), stated with the design, the models carry no topographic
predictors, because each trial enters once per macroregion (see *Model structure*).

One further covariate enters the ERP models. It is the L1 Dominance Score, the
per-participant derived score of that name in the Language History Questionnaire's
Aggregate Scores export [LHQ3: @lhq3], read from that export and $z$-standardised with the
other continuous predictors. It indexes how far the first language dominates the
participant's repertoire, and it is carried in the ERP models as a control for prior
language experience. In the extraction code, the variable carries the name of the
multilingual language diversity score, a legacy of an earlier version of the export in which
the two scores sat in different columns, so the label and the quantity modelled differ. The
models use the score described here. One participant had no questionnaire record. Because the score
serves only as a control, that participant was given the mean of the other participants'
scores (zero after standardisation), so that none of their trials was lost to the missing
covariate. Because single-trial amplitudes are $z$-scored within participant (below), this
between-participant score, like the language main effect, is identified only through the
imbalance of trials across each participant's conditions and sessions, and because it
enters no interaction it adjusts none of the grammaticality effects we interpret. The
covariate is not carried into the accuracy models. That asymmetry has no justification, and
we return to it in the Limitations.

The response side has two standardisation decisions of its own. Single-trial
amplitudes were $z$-scored within participant. The reasoning is the one @faust1999
set out for response latencies. When individuals differ in the overall scale of a
measure, and those differences are roughly linear, a group whose scale is larger
will show a larger raw treatment effect, and the resulting overadditive interaction
is an artefact of scale. They recommend a within-individual $z$ transformation as
the remedy. Single-trial ERP amplitude has the same property, and the risk applies
directly here because the language contrast is between participants, so a scale
difference between the two groups could otherwise present as a grammaticality
$\times$ language interaction.
We also entered the trial's own
pre-stimulus mean amplitude ($-100$ to $0$ ms) as a within-participant $z$-scored
covariate. Subtraction of a baseline is the special case of this model in which the
baseline coefficient is fixed at one. Estimating that coefficient lets the model absorb
baseline variance that subtraction would leave in the residual, which @alday2019
shows can raise power. It also avoids the assumption subtraction requires, that conditions
do not differ systematically during the baseline interval.

### Model structure

For each ERP cell (property $\times$ window $\times$ macroregion), we fitted a
Gaussian model of single-trial mean amplitude:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{amplitude} \sim\; & \text{baseline} + \text{Gram} \times \text{Session} \times \text{Language}
 + \text{L1 dominance} \\
 & + (1 + \text{Gram} \times \text{Session} \mid \text{participant}) + (1 + \text{Gram} + \text{Session} \mid \text{item}).
\end{aligned}
$$
Each trial enters once per model. The electrode clusters of a macroregion record the same
trial, and their amplitudes are correlated (between .45 and .64 in these data), so entering
them as separate rows would treat one trial as several independent observations. That
pseudoreplication [@lazic2010] narrows the intervals of every trial-level term, and here it
narrowed those of the grammaticality $\times$ session interaction and its interaction with
language by a factor of 1.4 to 2.0. Averaging the clusters within each trial removes it, and
the scalp distribution of the effects is described separately (see *Topography*).

For each property, we fitted a Bernoulli (logit-link) model of judgement accuracy
[@jaeger2008; @dixon2008]:
$$
\text{correct} \sim \text{Gram} \times \text{Session} \times \text{Language}
 + (1 + \text{Gram} + \text{Session} \mid \text{participant}).
$$

Participants and items are crossed rather than hierarchically nested. Within a
language, every participant sees every sentence frame, and every frame is seen by every
participant in that language, so the ERP models carry crossed by-participant and by-item
random effects [@baayen2008; @barr2013]. Items are nested within language, because the
two miniature languages draw on separate lexicons, so language does not vary within an
item and no by-item language slope is estimable. Grammaticality and session, by contrast,
vary within both grouping factors, since every frame is presented in both a grammatical
and an ungrammatical version and is re-presented across sessions.

Random effects therefore follow the "keep it maximal *as justified by the design*"
principle [@barr2013], so both grouping factors receive a random intercept plus
grammaticality and session slopes, with correlations estimated under the shared
$\mathrm{LKJ}(2)$ prior. Participants also receive a slope for the grammaticality
$\times$ session interaction, because the development of each participant's grammaticality
effect is the within-participant quantity on which the language-conditioned interaction
rests, and omitting that slope would make the interval of the fixed interaction too narrow
[@barr2013; @brauer2018].

Session enters that specification as a single linear predictor, so the change in the
grammaticality effect across the retention interval is read off the fitted trend rather
than estimated for that interval on its own. Gender agreement and differential object
marking were therefore also refitted with a binary indicator for the retention session,
interacted with grammaticality and language and added to the linear session term. The
linear term then carries the training trend and the indicator the deviation at Session 6.
The indicator is coded $+0.5$ at Session 6 and $-0.5$ elsewhere and, unlike the other
predictors, is not standardised, so its coefficient is the deviation at Session 6 on the
response scale. The refits are otherwise identical to the models above and were run
under both random-effect structures. Verb--object number agreement admits no such refit. It is
sampled at the two bracketing sessions only, so an indicator for the later of them would
be collinear with the linear term. Where the two derivations disagree, the freed estimate
is the one that bears on consolidation, and both are reported (@tbl-retention,
@tbl-retention-free).

The case for retaining the by-item grammaticality slope, and the power-based argument
against maximal structures that it was weighed against [@barr2013; @matuschek2017], are
set out in @apx-analytic-decisions-in-detail. The Results report the whole grid refitted without that slope, so
a reader can see which conclusions depend on it. The reported accuracy models carry
by-participant random effects only, although the judgement trials share the ERP models'
item factor, the sentence frame: `r item_inventory_clause()`. Leaving that factor out treats
the trials of one frame as independent, and because each frame belongs to one miniature
language, the group contrasts in sensitivity and criterion are also contrasts between two
sets of frames [@baayen2008; @barr2013]. Each accuracy model was therefore refitted with the
ERP models' by-item term, a by-frame intercept with grammaticality and session slopes, both
on its own and together with the by-participant grammaticality $\times$ session slope
described below. These refits are sensitivity analyses specified after the reported models
had been fitted.

### Signal-detection reading of the judgement models

A model of accuracy that includes grammaticality as a predictor is a logistic
signal-detection model in another parameterisation [@decarlo1998]. Let $H$ be the rate of
answering "grammatical" to a grammatical sentence (a hit) and $F$ the rate of answering
"grammatical" to an ungrammatical one (a false alarm). Accuracy on grammatical sentences is
$H$, and accuracy on ungrammatical sentences is $1 - F$. With grammaticality coded
symmetrically, the terms of the accuracy model that do not contain grammaticality (the
intercept, session, language and session $\times$ language) are half the logit-scale
sensitivity, $\operatorname{logit}H - \operatorname{logit}F$, and its change with session
and language. The terms that do contain grammaticality are half of
$\operatorname{logit}H + \operatorname{logit}F$, a response bias: a learner inclined to answer
"grammatical" gains accuracy on grammatical sentences and loses it on ungrammatical ones
without discriminating any better. The grammaticality $\times$ language and grammaticality
$\times$ session $\times$ language terms therefore index a between-language difference in
bias and in its development, not in discrimination. We report both quantities, derived for
each language and session as linear combinations of the posterior draws: sensitivity
$d_L = \operatorname{logit}H - \operatorname{logit}F$, and the criterion
$c_L = -(\operatorname{logit}H + \operatorname{logit}F)/2$, which is negative for a
readiness to answer "grammatical" [@macmillan2005]. On the logit scale, $d_L$ is about 1.7
times the familiar probit $d'$ [@decarlo1998]. For display, $d'$ and $c$ were also computed
per participant and session with the log-linear correction for extreme rates [@hautus1995].
The models were specified with the grammaticality terms read as discrimination, and
*Transparency, preregistration and analysis status* records when and why that reading was
replaced.

The reported accuracy models include by-participant slopes for grammaticality and for
session but not for their interaction, although that interaction, the within-participant
change in bias, varies within participants. Omitting such a slope can make the
corresponding fixed effect's interval too narrow [@barr2013]. Each accuracy model was
therefore refitted with the interaction slope added, as a sensitivity analysis specified
after the signal-detection reading above. With that slope, the refit is the
signal-detection model of the response itself in a different parameterisation: its
by-participant intercept and session slope are each learner's sensitivity and its change,
its by-participant grammaticality and grammaticality $\times$ session slopes are each
learner's criterion and its change, and the map between the two parameterisations is linear
and invertible, so the two models can differ only through their priors.

### Priors

We placed informative priors derived from the
morphosyntactic-ERP and behavioural literature, in place of the common
weakly informative default, following a selective, sign-informed and
magnitude-regularising strategy [@schad2021]. Because the response and all predictors
are standardised, each coefficient is expressed in standard-deviation units (within
participant, for the ERP models). A prior *mean* can therefore encode the direction of a
well-established effect, while its *standard deviation* stays wide enough to let the data
dominate any well-identified effect [@gelman2008].

The one firmly established directional effect is the P600: words that violate the
syntactic structure of a sentence elicit a late positivity, larger for ungrammatical than
for grammatical sentences [@osterhout1992]. For morphosyntactic violations specifically,
that positivity is posterior and centroparietal, and it is obtained in native speakers
[@mueller2005; @mueller2007; @chen2007] and, once some proficiency has been reached, in
artificial-language learners [@morganshort2010; @morganshort2012]. A P600 also
arises to structural violations in implicit artificial-grammar learning, where the
sequences carry no morphology at all [@silva2017]. Because
grammaticality is coded grammatical $=+0.5$, this implies a *negative* prior mean on the
grammaticality slope in the P600 window, carried more mildly into the 300--600 ms window
for the two agreement properties, whose late signature is a positivity rather than an N400.
For differential object marking, the specification differs in both windows, being widened
in the later window and left zero-centred in the earlier one, because case-marking
violations are configuration-dependent and elicit a P600, an N400 or a biphasic response
according to animacy and markedness [@nieuwland2013; @frisch2001; @mueller2007]. The early
(200--500 ms) anterior-negativity window was left zero-centred, because the LAN is small and
present in only roughly half of participants and items, so its sign is not safely
predictable [@caffarra2019]. The grammaticality
$\times$ session $\times$ language interaction, the language-conditioned contrast under test, was
kept zero-centred, because the second-language signature of these effects is qualitatively
contested [@chen2007; @mueller2009] and proficiency-dependent [@caffarra2015]. The priors
thus inform the model where the evidence is strong without biasing the effects we set out
to estimate.

For the accuracy models, artificial-language learners judge grammaticality well above
chance and improve across successive test blocks even under mere exposure, without
explicit instruction or feedback [@mueller2009], motivating a positive intercept and a
