positive session slope. In signal-detection terms, these encode above-chance sensitivity
that increases with training. Every term that carries grammaticality, and so indexes
response bias, received the zero-centred default. Random-effect standard deviations, and the residual standard
deviation of the ERP models, received a generous half--Student-$t$ prior, a weakly
informative default for variance parameters in hierarchical models [@gelman2006].
A generous prior is warranted here because between-participant variation in
the morphosyntactic ERP response is not incidental noise. @tanner2014 found that although
the grand mean showed the usual biphasic LAN--P600 pattern, individual responses varied
systematically along a continuum between negativity-dominant and positivity-dominant, so
participants differ in the form of the response and not only in its size. Modelling that
variation as a random effect over single trials, instead of averaging across it, is the
approach @volpertesmond2021 set out for ERP data. Random-effect correlation
matrices received an $\mathrm{LKJ}(2)$ prior [@lewandowski2009]. @tbl-priors in
@apx-prior-specifications gives the distribution placed on every parameter. The literature does not
supply a defensible microvolt effect size for these components (even systematic resampling
finds the magnitude of the P600 to vary widely across samples, @kim2024).
Prior means therefore encode only sign and a regularised magnitude, and their influence is
bounded by deliberately wide standard deviations. Prior
predictive simulation confirmed that the priors imply amplitude and accuracy distributions
that encompass the observed data (@fig-priorpc). Every model in the grid, under both
random-effect structures, and every accuracy model was also refitted on the same data,
as a sensitivity analysis, under the former weakly informative priors of
$\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and $\mathcal{N}(0, 1.5)$, and the estimates were essentially
unchanged.`r retfree_weak_note()` The largest
shift in any grammaticality term was `r prior_shift_max()` on the within-participant
standardised scale for the ERP models and `r prior_shift_max(family = "^accuracy_")` in
log-odds for the accuracy models. No grammaticality term's credible interval changed
width by more than `r prior_width_dev()`% in the ERP models or
`r prior_width_dev(family = "^accuracy_")`% in the accuracy models. Taken over every
reported parameter, the largest width change
was `r prior_width_dev(pattern = "", family = "")`%. The informative priors therefore regularise without driving the
conclusions [@schad2021; @depaoli2017; @vandeschoot2021]. Under both random-effect
structures, each grammaticality term is credible in the same ERP cells, with the same sign,
under the weak priors as under the informative
ones.`r cred_agree_guard("_weakprior_itemslope", "_itemslope")``r cred_agree_guard("_weakprior", "")`
The credible effect whose interval lies closest to zero (gender agreement, grammaticality
$\times$ session, midline 400--900 ms) is
`r report_effect("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_midline_weakprior_itemslope", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session")`
under the weak priors, so its credibility does not depend on them.

```{r}
#| include: false
# The prior predictive check, drawn here from the two tables that
# scripts/03b_export_prior_predictive.R writes (hpc/03b_prior_predictive.slurm): the
# kernel densities of the observed amplitudes and of each dataset simulated from the
# priors, over the displayed range, and a one-row record of the run. Until 26 October 2026
# the figure was a bayesplot PNG that only the fitting script could redraw. The note's
# numbers come from the record, so they cannot outlive a rerun.
.ppc_tbl  <- .read_csv_if(paper1_results("_prior_predictive_check.csv"))
.ppc_meta <- .read_csv_if(paper1_results("_prior_predictive_check_meta.csv"))
priorpc_note <- function() {
  m <- .ppc_meta
  ok <- !is.null(m) && nrow(m) == 1L &&
    all(c("ndraws", "n_obs", "x_max", "abs_q99", "share_within") %in% names(m))
  paste0(
    "The model is subject--verb gender agreement, 400--900 ms, midline, with its informative ",
    "priors and the maximal random-effect structure. ",
    if (ok) sprintf("Grey lines are the densities of %d datasets simulated from the priors alone, with the likelihood switched off, and the black line is that of the %s observed single-trial amplitudes, z-scored within participant. ",
                    as.integer(m$ndraws), format(m$n_obs, big.mark = ","))
    else "Grey lines are the densities of datasets simulated from the priors alone, with the likelihood switched off, and the black line is that of the observed single-trial amplitudes, z-scored within participant. ",
    "Each density is a Gaussian kernel estimate. The horizontal axis is amplitude in ",
    "within-participant standard deviations and the vertical axis is density. The prior ",
    "predictive distribution comfortably encompasses the observed data, so the priors are not ",
    "in conflict with it. ",
    if (ok) sprintf("The horizontal axis is limited to %s standard deviations either side of zero, which holds %s%% of the simulated values. Wide priors on a standardised scale are meant to reach far: 1%% of the simulated values lie beyond %s, and on that range the observed density would collapse to a spike at zero. ",
                    format(m$x_max), apa_num(100 * m$share_within, digits = 0),
                    apa_num(m$abs_q99, digits = 0))
    else "",
    "The check therefore establishes that the priors generate data of a plausible order of ",
    "magnitude, not that they are tightly calibrated to the observed distribution.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-priorpc
#| fig-cap: "Prior Predictive Check for a Representative ERP Model"
#| apa-note: !expr priorpc_note()
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: !expr if (!is.null(.ppc_tbl)) 3.2 else 1
# Without the else branch, a checkout that lacks the tables emits nothing at all and the
# cross-reference in the text above renders as a dangling "?@fig-priorpc".
if (!is.null(.ppc_tbl)) {
  .obs <- .ppc_tbl[.ppc_tbl$series == "observed", , drop = FALSE]
  .pri <- .ppc_tbl[.ppc_tbl$series == "prior", , drop = FALSE]
  # Direct labels in place of a key, as in the other figures: the observed curve beside its
  # peak, and the simulated datasets above their band on the right.
  .pk <- .obs[which.max(.obs$density), , drop = FALSE]
  .bx <- 0.55 * max(.ppc_tbl$x)
  .by <- max(.pri$density[abs(.pri$x - .bx) <= diff(range(.ppc_tbl$x)) / 100])
  ggplot() +
    geom_line(data = .pri, aes(x, density, group = draw), colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.25) +
    geom_line(data = .obs, aes(x, density), colour = "#000000", linewidth = 2 * LES_LWD) +
    annotate("text", x = .pk$x + 0.6, y = 0.9 * .pk$density, label = "Observed amplitudes",
             hjust = 0, colour = LES_INK) +
    annotate("text", x = .bx, y = .by + 0.04 * .pk$density, label = "Simulated from the priors",
             hjust = 0.5, vjust = 0, colour = LES_INK) +
    # True minus signs on the axis, as in the other figures, and a y range that starts at
    # zero so that its tick is labelled (the smallest density is a hair above zero).
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-8, 8, 2), labels = les_lab_num,
                       expand = expansion(mult = 0.01)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.04))) +
    labs(x = "Single-trial amplitude (within-participant SD units)", y = "Density") +
    les_theme(grid = "y")
} else {
  les_placeholder("Prior predictive check pending its export (scripts/03b_export_prior_predictive.R)")
}
```

### Sampler settings and convergence

Each model was run with four chains of 10,000 iterations, the first 2,000 of each
discarded as warm-up, with `adapt_delta = 0.95` and `max_treedepth = 12` to accommodate the
challenging geometry of maximal multilevel posteriors.`r iter_exceptions()` Convergence was assessed
with the rank-normalised split-$\widehat{R}$ and bulk/tail effective sample sizes
[@vehtari2021], requiring $\widehat{R} < 1.01$, bulk- and tail-ESS $> 400$, and
no divergent transitions. Model fit was checked with posterior predictive checks
[@gabry2019]. These two thresholds do different jobs. An
effective sample size of 400 (at least 100 per chain) is the point at which the
$\widehat{R}$ and ESS diagnostics are themselves reliable [@vehtari2021]. The stability of a
95% interval limit is a more demanding requirement, because extreme quantiles are estimated
far less efficiently than a posterior mean [@kruschke2021]. Over all parameters of all
models, the smallest bulk effective sample size is `r conv_min_ess("bulk")` and the smallest
tail effective sample size is `r conv_min_ess("tail")`, with the per-model values in
@tbl-convergence-appendix and @tbl-convergence-accuracy in @apx-convergence-diagnostics.
At the lower end of that range, the margin over the floor of 400 is narrow. The interval
limits of those models are therefore estimated less precisely than their medians, and
coefficients whose intervals lie close to zero should be treated as
borderline.

### Inference

We summarise each effect by its posterior median, 95% credible interval (CrI) and
probability of direction ($p_d$, the posterior probability that the effect has its
median's sign), an estimation-first approach that avoids dichotomous
null-hypothesis testing [@makowski2019]. We describe an effect as *credible* when its 95%
credible interval excludes zero, and otherwise read $p_d$ as a continuous index of
directional certainty [@kruschke2018]. All
credible intervals are equal-tailed quantile intervals bounded by the 2.5th and 97.5th
percentiles of the posterior draws. For a skewed
posterior, an equal-tailed and a highest-density interval can differ in whether they
contain zero, so the choice is stated [@kruschke2021]. Within each model, hierarchical shrinkage
across participants and items already regularises the coefficient estimates
[@kruschke2018; @gelmanhillyajima2012]. The eighteen cells are fitted separately and are
not pooled towards one another, so that shrinkage is not itself an argument about the grid. The grid (3
properties $\times$ 3 a priori windows $\times$ 2 macroregions) is fixed before
fitting, and no cell is screened for significance before it is reported (@fig-erp-forest
reports all 18 cells for the four grammaticality terms, and @tbl-retention the derived
retention contrasts). No correction across cells is applied. Where a
conclusion does rest on particular cells crossing the credibility threshold, we treat it as
provisional on that basis (see *Strength of evidence* in the Discussion). We do not claim
the grid is immune to selection effects [@rubin2021].
The derived retention effect (Session 4 $\to$
Session 6) and its language-scoped contrasts are posterior quantities computed from
the same models, summarised and disclosed in full the same way (@tbl-retention). For
gender agreement and differential object marking, they are also re-estimated in refits that
free the Session-6 step from the training trend, described under *Model structure*
(@tbl-retention-free).

### Multivariate decoding of grammaticality

The Bayesian models above summarise each trial by its mean amplitude over a
macroregion, which could miss a grammaticality signal that is distributed across the
scalp too weakly to move any single cluster's mean but is nonetheless jointly
decodable from the whole-scalp pattern [@haxby2001]. As a complementary,
classical (non-Bayesian) analysis, we decoded Grammatical from
Ungrammatical trials directly from the single-trial amplitude pattern across all
EEG sensors at every time sample, downsampled to a 4 ms grid, after subtracting from each
sensor the trial's mean over the 100 ms before the critical word. The amplitude models enter
that mean as a covariate instead [@alday2019]. Subtraction moves the conditions' difference in
that mean into every later sample of the decoder's input, with its sign reversed.
The classifier was a
regularised linear discriminant analysis under leave-one-participant-out
cross-validation, a time-resolved multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA)
approach for EEG/MEG [@grootswagers2017]. Leave-one-participant-out is the
generalisation test this question calls for, since what is at stake is whether the
pattern transfers to an unseen learner. @varoquaux2017 show that leave-one-out
schemes give more variable accuracy estimates than repeated random splits, so we read
the AUC time-course below as a profile whose individual point estimates carry limited
precision. Decoding performance is
summarised as the area under the ROC curve (AUC) at each time point. Chance-level
calibration was established with a permutation test that shuffles the
grammaticality labels once per permutation, holding the shuffle constant across the
whole time-course so that the null preserves each trial's temporal autocorrelation.
Multiple comparisons across time points were corrected with cluster-based
permutation inference [@maris2007]. Clusters were formed from temporally contiguous
samples whose AUC exceeded the 95th percentile of the pooled permutation null, the
cluster statistic was the summed excess of AUC over that threshold, and each cluster
was assessed against the distribution of the largest cluster statistic across
permutations. A second correction layer, for the false-discovery
rate (FDR), is applied across clusters, with the family defined per property. Benjamini--Hochberg
correction ($q < .05$) is applied across the clusters of a
property's pooled overall time-course, and each property's family is corrected
separately. A Benjamini--Hochberg adjustment never lowers a $p$ value, so this second layer
can only remove clusters that pass the maximum-cluster test, and because that test already
controls the family-wise error rate across time, the layer adds no error control of its
own. We therefore report the clusters that pass the first test alongside those that survive
both. The session-resolved and session-by-language breakdowns carry only their own
cluster-level $p$ values. @apx-analytic-decisions-in-detail sets out why the family is defined this way.
Grammatical and ungrammatical trial counts differ
across participants and decline across sessions, so we balanced the classes by
undersampling the majority class within each participant of the training fold. The
discriminant's pooled within-class covariance was ridged by one thousandth of its mean
diagonal for numerical stability. The time-course AUC, computed within each held-out
participant, is in any case insensitive to class prevalence, so neither the classifier nor
the metric can exploit a prevalence shortcut there, and chance was set by the empirical
within-participant permutation null [@combrisson2015]. The labels were shuffled within
participant and not within each session, which the design allows because the two
conditions were presented in near-equal numbers at every session. The
permutation null comprised `r n_perm_txt()` shufflings, so the smallest attainable cluster
$p$ is `r min_cluster_p()`. This bounds the resolution of near-threshold cluster $p$-values,
and the surviving clusters are reported with that granularity in mind [@nichols2002;
@phipson2010].`r decode_status_method()` The
decoder is given the EEG sensors alone. The amplifier's built-in accelerometer
channels are excluded, as is any channel not exported for every session a property
was recorded in, so that each property's pattern is brain-derived and no sensor is
present for one session's trials but structurally absent for another's. Beyond the overall time-course, five further analyses were run. Decoding separately
by session, and by session $\times$ mini-language, gives a multivariate analogue of
the ERP models' grammaticality $\times$ session and $\times$ language terms. A
cross-language generalisation analysis trains the decoder on one mini-language and
tests it on the other. A cross-property generalisation analysis trains on one grammatical
property's Grammatical/Ungrammatical contrast and tests on another. Finally, temporal generalisation trains a decoder at every time
point and tests it at every other, on a grid coarsened by a factor of two on both axes to
keep the computation tractable. It characterises whether the same neural code is
stable across the epoch or evolves [@king2014]. The two generalisation analyses carry no
permutation null and are reported as descriptive comparisons. Cross-validating strictly
out-of-participant throughout guards against the circular, non-independent analysis
that would otherwise inflate apparent decoding accuracy [@kriegeskorte2009].

## Transparency, preregistration and analysis status

The study design, artificial-language materials and session protocol were
preregistered before data collection (<https://osf.io/tjr54>). The preregistration
specified the design, the miniature-language materials, the six-session schedule and
the EEG acquisition, but it did not commit to a statistical analysis plan. The
Bayesian multilevel models, the literature-derived informative priors, the latency
windows and macroregions, the Session 4 $\to$ 6 retention contrasts and the
multivariate decoding analyses reported here were therefore specified after the data
were collected. None was preregistered, so all are exploratory in the registered
sense, and we report them as estimation-oriented analyses, since none tests a
preregistered hypothesis [@nosek2018; @wagenmakers2012]. Within that frame,
we distinguish *primary* from *secondary* analyses. The primary analyses, fixed
before any model was fitted, comprise the ERP grid of properties, windows,
macroregions and priors together with the pooled, all-sessions decoding time-course
for each property. The secondary analyses are the session-resolved and
session-by-language decoding breakdowns, the cross-language and cross-property
generalisation analyses, and the temporal-generalisation matrix. What the
paper reports of them varies, and we say which is which. The cross-language and
cross-property peaks are quoted in the Results. The session-resolved and
session-by-language breakdowns and the temporal-generalisation matrices are not summarised
numerically here and are available in the deposited decoding artefacts`r if (decode_runs_pending()) paste0(", those of ", .decode_runs_pending_txt(), " once their runs finish") else ""`. Where a secondary
analysis carries a cluster-level $p$ value, that value is family-wise-error-controlled over
time in the usual way, but none of them is treated as a test of the paper's claims. Where the decoding analyses
speak of a "confirmatory family", the term names the false-discovery-rate correction
family (the clusters of each property's pooled overall time-course), not
preregistered confirmation. On a minor point of adherence, a third, ancillary violation
type was recorded per property but, as noted above, is not analysed here.

Several decisions were made after results had been inspected, and we label them as such.
First, peak decoding accuracies are quoted on the post-stimulus axis, a restriction adopted
once the pre-stimulus interval was found not to be at chance for differential object
marking. The pre-stimulus interval is retained and reported alongside as a negative control.
Second, the temporal-generalisation and cross-property analyses were reclassified as
descriptive after it became clear that no null distribution had been computed for them.
Third, the judgement models were first read with their grammaticality terms as
discrimination. We later recognised that, with accuracy as the response, those terms index
response bias (see *Signal-detection reading of the judgement models*), and the behavioural
results are reported in signal-detection terms throughout. The models themselves were not
changed. The refit adding a by-participant slope for the change in bias was specified at
the same point, as a sensitivity analysis. Fourth, an audit of the archived EEG processing
histories found five Session 3 recordings, beyond the four already excluded, that had been
filtered at 1 Hz. All nine were reprocessed at 0.1 Hz under a protocol fixed before any
reprocessed output was inspected, and the protocol's robustness analysis refits the ERP
models without them (see *EEG acquisition and single-trial ERP quantification*). The same
audit found three exports that do not contain the participant-session they are named for, of
which two were recovered under that protocol and the third is excluded. It also found that
the Session 2 recordings had been re-referenced differently from the
others, which we corrected, and identified the participant trained in the wrong miniature
language at Session 2, who is excluded (see *Participants*). All of these decisions rest on
how the data were collected or processed, not on the values of the data. Fifth, the Introduction's statement of what the transfer accounts
predict was revised after the results were known, when it became clear that the lexical
and structural differences between the two miniature languages do not separate the
accounts as the original framing assumed. The revised statement sets out the predictions
each account makes for the design as it was run, including those our results contradict.
Sixth, the ERP models first entered each trial once per electrode cluster. A check of their
residual structure after the first fits showed that one trial's observations across
clusters were correlated, so those models overstated the precision of the trial-level
terms, and the models were respecified with one observation per trial per macroregion and
a by-participant slope
for the grammaticality $\times$ session interaction (see *Model structure*). The change was
made on statistical grounds and before the Bayesian models were refitted. In frequentist
(lme4) fits of the same data, it widened the intervals of the language-conditioned terms,
which the earlier specification had reported as credible in several cells. In the respecified
models, fitted to the corrected sample, no language-conditioned term is credible in any
cell.`r cred_cells_guard("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language", character(0))``r cred_cells_guard("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language", character(0))`
Seventh, the false-discovery-rate family of the decoding analyses was narrowed in July 2026
to the clusters of each property's pooled time-course, after a run under a wider family that
also spanned the session-resolved breakdowns had been inspected. Correcting across those
nested re-analyses of the same trials leaves the number of hypotheses undefined (see
@apx-analytic-decisions-in-detail). The second layer itself was kept, after the corrected
sample's results were seen, as it had been specified, and the clusters that pass the first
layer alone are reported beside it. Eighth, the judgements were first analysed under a
reaction-time screen carried over from the project's earlier preprocessing. After the
accuracy models had been fitted both with and without it, we examined what the screen
removes. It removes the most and the least accurate judgements, and a larger share of the
Mini-English group's judgements than of the Mini-Norwegian group's (see
*Grammaticality-judgement task*). We therefore stopped applying it. The fits with it are
reported as a sensitivity analysis, and the results that only one of the two fits supports
are graded as suggestive (see *Strength of evidence*). The refits on every judgement with the
other random-effect structures, priors and covariate were run after this decision. In the
refit that adds a by-participant slope for the change in bias, the gender-agreement criterion
difference was credible `r sdt_language_clause_model("criterion", "_maxranef")`, which is why
that difference is graded as suggestive.
None of these decisions creates a new test of the paper's claims.`r decode_status_transparency()`

The preregistration planned data collection at two sites, in Norway and Spain. The
present analyses concern only the Norwegian cohort (first-language Norwegian,
second-language English learners of Mini-English or Mini-Norwegian). The Spanish-site
data are not analysed here. The findings therefore speak to
first-language-Norwegian learners, and generalisation to the other registered
populations is an open question.

The preregistered protocol required participants to score above 80% on the post-training
behavioural test in each grammar session before proceeding to the EEG experiment. After
a few participants had been tested, we recognised that this criterion was too strict and
modified the procedure: when the first test score was below 80%, pretraining, training
and the test were repeated; after the second attempt, participants proceeded to the
experiment regardless of their score. Participants were shown their percentage correct
at the end of each test attempt. The 80% threshold therefore describes the first-attempt
gate, not a requirement imposed on the second attempt. This performance threshold is
both an inclusion criterion and a performance-conditional missingness mechanism, since
it conditions which participant-sessions contribute EEG and behaviour. Its effect is
therefore folded into the attendance counts in @fig-flow, which record who contributed
data at each stage but not why. Whether each participant met the threshold at a given
session is not reported. It can only be reconstructed from the final pass record in the
training logs, and that reconstruction does not reconcile with the attendance counts at
Session 4, so we do not quote numbers from it.

# Results

```{r}
#| results: asis
# Convergence is reported as a worst case in one sentence rather than as a table of one
# row per fit. The population is 18 ERP cells under two random-effect structures and two
# prior sets (72), plus 3 accuracy models -- which have a single structure, since no
# by-item term is identifiable for them -- under the two prior sets (6), plus the
# retention-free refits of the 12 gender-agreement and differential-object-marking cells
# under both structures with the informative priors (24), and the further sensitivity
# refits. A table of one row per fit would be that many rows of near-identical numbers.
# The extreme value over all of them carries the same information: if the worst R-hat is
# below the threshold then so is every other. The per-model values are in the two tables
# of the convergence appendix (ERP fits, then judgement-accuracy fits), which mark any fit
# that did not meet the criteria. The count is taken from the artefact rather than typed,
# so it cannot drift when the grid is extended (as it was by the refits).
if (!is.null(conv_tbl)) {
  np <- sum(conv_tbl$passed, na.rm = TRUE)
  n_fit <- nrow(conv_tbl)
  # Only claim "all" when all of them passed; otherwise state the proportion, so a single
  # failing refit cannot render as "All N met the criteria. 1 model did not meet it."
  # The divergence clause is built the same way. It was written as a flat assertion, which
  # was true of the grid as first fitted. A refit that diverged would have printed a
  # falsehood next to a table marking that very fit. A divergence is recorded against a
  # model that failed the gate, so it is stated in its own sentence rather than appended
  # to the list of criteria the passing models met.
  n_div <- sum(conv_tbl$n_divergent, na.rm = TRUE)
  clean <- all(!is.na(conv_tbl$n_divergent)) && n_div == 0
  cat(sprintf(paste0(
    "%s met the convergence criteria. Taken over every parameter of every ",
    "model, the largest rank-normalised $\\widehat{R}$ was %.3f, the smallest bulk and ",
    "tail effective sample sizes were %s and %s%s. Per-model values are given in ",
    "@tbl-convergence-appendix and @tbl-convergence-accuracy.\n"),
    if (np == n_fit) sprintf("All %d fitted models", n_fit)
    else sprintf("%d of the %d fitted models", np, n_fit),
    max(conv_tbl$max_rhat, na.rm = TRUE),
    format(round(min(conv_tbl$min_ess_bulk, na.rm = TRUE)), big.mark = ","),
    format(round(min(conv_tbl$min_ess_tail, na.rm = TRUE)), big.mark = ","),
    if (clean) ", and no model produced a divergent transition" else ""))
  if (!clean) {
    # A count that opens a sentence is spelled out (APA 7). Kept local to this manuscript
    # rather than put in _shared/R/, which cannot be redeployed to the cluster while the
    # Paper 1 jobs are live.
    n_div_mod <- sum(conv_tbl$n_divergent > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
    .spell <- function(n) c("One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five", "Six", "Seven",
                            "Eight", "Nine", "Ten")[n]
    cat(sprintf(" %s produced %s.\n",
                if (n_div_mod == 1L) "One model"
                else paste(if (n_div_mod <= 10L) .spell(n_div_mod)
                           else format(n_div_mod, big.mark = ","), "models"),
                if (n_div == 1L) "a single divergent transition"
                else sprintf("%s divergent transitions in total",
                             format(n_div, big.mark = ","))))
  }
  if (np < n_fit) {
    # Refer to the table(s) that hold the marked fits. Two are written as two full
    # references ("Table D1 and Table D2"): apaquarto-docx ignores the prefix
    # suppression of [-@...], so "Tables [-@a] and [-@b]" prints "Tables Table D1 and
    # Table D2" in Word, and a grouped reference prints "Table D1, Table D2".
    fail_erp <- startsWith(conv_tbl$model, "erp_")[!is.na(conv_tbl$passed) & !conv_tbl$passed]
    where <- c(if (any(fail_erp)) "tbl-convergence-appendix",
               if (any(!fail_erp)) "tbl-convergence-accuracy")
    cat(sprintf(" The remaining %s marked with a superscript *a* in %s.\n",
                if (n_fit - np == 1L) "model is" else sprintf("%d models are", n_fit - np),
                if (length(where)) paste0("@", where, collapse = " and ")
                else "the tables of the convergence appendix"))
  }
} else {
  cat("*Convergence diagnostics will appear here once the models are fitted.*\n")
}
```

## ERP signatures of grammatical processing and their development

We assess, for each property, whether it elicited a grammaticality effect, whether that
effect changed across sessions (the grammaticality $\times$ session interaction), and
whether the effect or its development was modulated by language (the grammaticality
$\times$ language and grammaticality $\times$ session $\times$ language interactions). The
pattern differs by property. Gender agreement showed a grammaticality effect in the early and
middle windows that grew across sessions in the late window, where the grammaticality
$\times$ session interaction was credible in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session", "gender_agreement")` cells;
differential object marking showed a transient early grammaticality effect; and verb--object
number agreement showed no credible effect (@fig-erp-forest). No term involving language was
credible for any property: the grammaticality $\times$ language interaction was credible in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language")` cells and the
grammaticality $\times$ session $\times$ language interaction in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`. The
same terms are credible, with the same signs, when the reprocessed and recovered records are
left out (@tbl-robustness).`r cred_agree_guard("_exclreproc_itemslope", "_itemslope")` The condition averages are shown for each miniature-language
group in @fig-erp-waveforms, the two groups' difference waves in
@fig-erp-difference-groups, and the scalp distribution of the effect in each group and
window in @fig-erp-topography.

One coding fact governs how every coefficient below should be read. A positive
grammaticality coefficient means that grammatical trials were more positive than
ungrammatical ones, because grammaticality is coded grammatical $= +0.5$. Violations
therefore appear as a relative negativity. The canonical P600 would produce a negative
coefficient. Every credible grammaticality effect below is positive, so the dominant
signature in these learners is a violation-related negativity where our priors
anticipated a late positivity, a point we return to in the Discussion. Results are
organised by property.

```{r}
#| label: fig-erp-forest
#| fig-cap: "Posterior Medians and 95% Credible Intervals of the Grammaticality Terms in Every ERP Cell"
#| apa-note: "Points are posterior medians and horizontal lines 95% equal-tailed credible intervals (CrI) for the four grammaticality terms of each single-trial ERP model (maximal random-effect structure, informative priors). The vertical grey line marks zero. Columns are grammatical properties and rows are model terms. Within each panel the three a priori windows run from earliest (top) to latest (bottom), with the midline estimate (circle) above the lateral one (square). Filled symbols mark intervals that exclude zero; open symbols, intervals that include it. All panels share one horizontal scale, in within-participant standard deviations of single-trial amplitude. Grammaticality (grammatical = +0.5) and language (Mini-Norwegian = +0.5) were coded before standardisation, so a positive grammaticality coefficient is a relative negativity for violations, and a positive term involving language is a larger value of the corresponding grammaticality term in the Mini-Norwegian group. Verb--object number agreement was recorded at Sessions 4 and 6 only, so its session terms index change across the retention interval."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: !expr if (erp_forest_ready) 6.3 else 1
# The note names the maximal structure and the informative priors because those are the
# fits kept below; if LES_P1_PRIMARY is switched to "base", change "maximal" in the note.
# Rows run from the grammaticality main effect through its two-way interactions with
# language and with session to the three-way term.
key_terms <- c("z_recoded_grammaticality",
               "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language",
               "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session",
               "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")
fp <- NULL
if (erp_forest_ready) {
  win_lab <- c(`200_500` = "200–500 ms", `300_600` = "300–600 ms",
               `400_900` = "400–900 ms")
  # Keep ONE fit per cell. post_tbl holds four variants of every cell -- the base and
  # maximal random-effect structures crossed with the informative and weak prior sets --
  # and without this filter all four were drawn at the same coordinates, so the figure
  # superimposed the reported fits on the sensitivity fits. Route through .mid() so the
  # figure follows LES_P1_PRIMARY rather than naming a structure here.
  fp <- post_tbl |>
    filter(parameter %in% key_terms, !startsWith(model, "accuracy_"), !.is_variant(model),
           model == vapply(sub("_itemslope$", "", model), .mid, "")) |>
    mutate(
      # Strip the structure suffix before parsing. The filter above keeps the primary
      # structure's ids, which under LES_P1_PRIMARY = "maximal" all end "_itemslope";
      # the patterns below anchor on a "(lateral|midline)$" ending, so parsing the
      # suffixed id would return it unchanged and every label would become NA.
      id       = sub("_itemslope$", "", gsub("^erp_", "", model)),
      Term     = factor(.pretty_term(parameter), levels = .pretty_term(key_terms)),
      Region   = factor(sub(".*_(lateral|midline)$", "\\1", id),
                        levels = c("midline", "lateral"), labels = c("Midline", "Lateral")),
      Window   = factor(unname(win_lab[sub(".*_([0-9]+_[0-9]+)_(lateral|midline)$", "\\1", id)]),
                        levels = unname(win_lab)),
      Property = les_property_factor(sub("_[0-9]+_[0-9]+_(lateral|midline)$", "", id)),
      Credible = (ci_low > 0) | (ci_high < 0),
      # Windows run from earliest (top) to latest; within a window the midline estimate
      # sits just above the lateral one.
      y        = (4 - as.integer(Window)) + ifelse(Region == "Midline", 0.17, -0.17))
  # 18 cells x 4 terms. Fewer rows mean a cell or term is missing from the artefact.
  if (nrow(fp) != 72L)
    warning("fig-erp-forest: ", nrow(fp), " estimates found, 72 expected")
}
if (!is.null(fp) && nrow(fp)) {
  ggplot(fp, aes(x = median, y = y)) +
    les_ref_v(0) +
    geom_linerange(aes(xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high), linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_point(aes(shape = Region, fill = Credible), size = 2, stroke = 0.6, colour = "black") +
    # Term strips break before each operator, one factor per line ("Grammaticality" /
    # "× Session" / "× Language"), so no line ends on a dangling "×".
    facet_grid(Term ~ Property, switch = "y",
               labeller = labeller(Term = function(x) gsub(" × ", "\n× ", x, fixed = TRUE),
                                   Property = les_wrap(18))) +
    # Macroregion is the one legend title kept: "Midline" and "Lateral" alone do not say
    # what they are levels of. Filled/open (credibility) is explained in the note.
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(Midline = 21, Lateral = 22), name = "Macroregion") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "black", `FALSE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = 3:1, labels = unname(win_lab), expand = expansion(add = 0.45)) +
    # One common horizontal scale, so magnitudes compare across properties and terms. The
    # breaks are pretty values clipped to the limits: breaks_extended(n = 3) chose -0.1, 0
    # and 0.1 for limits of about +/-0.07, and ggplot dropped the two outside them, which
    # left zero as the only labelled value and no way to read a magnitude off the axis.
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = function(lim) {
                         b <- pretty(lim, n = 4)
                         b[b >= lim[1] & b <= lim[2]]
                       }, labels = les_lab_num) +
    guides(shape = guide_legend(override.aes = list(fill = "black"))) +
    labs(x = "Coefficient (within-participant SD units)", y = NULL) +
    les_forest_theme() +
    # Wider column gaps keep the end ticks of neighbouring panels ("0.05", "-0.05") apart,
    # and bottom-aligned column strips put a one-line property name on the baseline of
    # the two-line ones.
    theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(14, "pt"), strip.text.x = element_text(vjust = 0))
} else {
  les_placeholder("ERP estimates withheld pending the refits")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-erp-waveforms
#| fig-cap: "Grand-Average ERPs by Electrode Cluster, Miniature Language and Property"
#| apa-note: "The upper block is a midline posterior electrode cluster, where the P600 is typically largest, and the lower block a left anterior cluster, where the LAN is typically largest (the models use macroregion means). Black lines are grammatical and green lines ungrammatical sentences, pooled over each property's sessions. Each participant's waveform was baseline-corrected ($-100$ to 0 ms) and averaged over their sessions before participants were averaged, so every participant carries equal weight. Ribbons are descriptive pointwise 95% normal intervals from the participant-level standard error. Positive is plotted up, and all panels share one scale. Grey bars mark the a priori windows (from the top, 200--500, 300--600 and 400--900 ms) and the triangle the median onset of the next word. The sample is the modelled one, and inferences rest on the models summarised in the forest plot of posterior estimates."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: !expr if (group_figures_ready) 6 else 1
# Sorted in byte order so the row order of the pooled frame does not depend on the
# collation of the rendering machine.
ga_files <- sort(list.files(paper1_results(), pattern = "^_grand_average_.*\\.csv$",
                            full.names = TRUE), method = "radix")
.props3 <- unname(LES_PROPERTY_LABELS)
.prop_factor <- function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x)
  m <- unname(LES_PROPERTY_LABELS[x])
  m[is.na(m)] <- x[is.na(m)]
  factor(m, levels = .props3)
}
.lang_levels <- LES_LANG_LEVELS
# The group colours are the house registry's LES_LANG_COLS (06_manuscript_helpers.R),
# Okabe-Ito blue and vermilion, the same in every group display of both papers.
.lang_cols <- LES_LANG_COLS
# Median onset of the word after the critical word (the RSVP timing census, read into
# .rsvp_tim in the setup chunk), marked by a triangle in the window gutter of every ERP
# time course. NA draws no triangle.
.next_word_ms <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.rsvp_tim[["next_onset_median_ms"]]))
if (length(.next_word_ms) != 1L) .next_word_ms <- NA_real_
# The two electrode-cluster blocks of the grand-average and difference-wave figures are
# stacked, each under a bold title. The upper block drops its x axis and the lower one its
# column strips, so the stack reads as one figure with one y-axis title and one legend,
# collected at the bottom left (a collected top legend would sit between the first
# block's title and its strips). The block titles start at the panels, clear of the
# collected y-axis title, and wrapped column strips sit on the panel edge. The stack
# itself takes the house theme, which sets the legend's spacing; patchwork would
# otherwise use ggplot2's default theme for it.
.erp_stack <- function(upper, lower) {
  upper <- upper + theme(axis.title.x = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank(),
                         axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), strip.text.x = element_text(vjust = 0))
  lower <- lower + theme(strip.text.x = element_blank())
  wrap_plots(upper, lower, ncol = 1) +
    plot_layout(guides = "collect", axis_titles = "collect") +
    plot_annotation(theme = les_theme()) &
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.justification = "left",
          plot.title.position = "panel")
}
reps <- c("midline posterior", "left anterior")
.site_factor <- function(x) factor(x, levels = reps, labels = c("Midline posterior", "Left anterior"))
ga <- if (group_figures_ready) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(ga_files, utils::read.csv, stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
} else NULL
if (!is.null(ga)) {
  gw <- ga[ga$brain_region %in% reps & ga$session == "pooled", ]
  gw$Site <- .site_factor(gw$brain_region)
  gw$Property <- les_property_factor(gw$grammatical_property)
  gw$Language <- factor(gw$mini_language, levels = .lang_levels)
  gw$grammaticality <- factor(gw$grammaticality, levels = LES_GRAM_LEVELS)
  # One y scale for every panel, taken from the data with the ribbons, so that no
  # reprocessed session can clip; the window bars sit in a gutter below it.
  fr8 <- les_erp_frame(min(gw$mean_amp - 1.96 * gw$se_amp),
                       max(gw$mean_amp + 1.96 * gw$se_amp), seq(-4, 8, 4))
  # Language is the row facet, so grammaticality takes colour alone (black and bluish
  # green), both lines solid; one scale keys line and ribbon together.
  blk <- function(site)
    ggplot(gw[gw$Site == site, ],
           aes(time, mean_amp, colour = grammaticality, fill = grammaticality)) +
      les_erp_layers(fr8, .next_word_ms) +
      geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean_amp - 1.96 * se_amp, ymax = mean_amp + 1.96 * se_amp),
                  alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
      geom_line(linewidth = LES_LWD_TRACE) +
      facet_grid(Language ~ Property, labeller = labeller(Property = les_wrap(20))) +
      les_scale_grammaticality() +
      labs(title = site, x = "Time from critical-word onset (ms)", y = "Amplitude (µV)") +
      les_theme()
  .erp_stack(blk("Midline posterior"), blk("Left anterior"))
} else {
  les_placeholder("Group-separated grand-average waveforms pending the updated extraction")
}
```

The grammaticality effect is easier to compare between the groups once the shared evoked
response is subtracted. @fig-erp-difference-groups overlays the two groups' difference
waves (ungrammatical minus grammatical) at the same two electrode clusters.

```{r}
#| label: fig-erp-difference-groups
#| fig-cap: "Difference Waves (Ungrammatical Minus Grammatical) by Electrode Cluster, Miniature Language and Property"
#| apa-note: "Each line is the participant-paired difference between ungrammatical and grammatical baseline-corrected waveforms, averaged over each participant's sessions and then over participants, for the Mini-Norwegian (blue) and Mini-English (vermilion) groups at the two electrode clusters of the grand-average figure. Values below zero mark a relative negativity for violations, the opposite sign to the grammaticality coefficient in the models, where grammatical is coded +0.5. Ribbons are pointwise 95% normal intervals from the participant-level standard error of the paired difference. Positive is plotted up. Grey bars mark the a priori windows and the triangle the median onset of the next word, as in the grand-average figure. Session-resolved difference waves are given in the appendix on group displays by session."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: !expr if (group_figures_ready) 4.4 else 1
# dwv is reused by the session-resolved difference waves in the appendix.
dwv <- if (group_figures_ready) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(.group_dw_files, utils::read.csv, stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
} else NULL
if (!is.null(dwv)) {
  dp <- dwv[dwv$brain_region %in% reps & dwv$session == "pooled", ]
  dp$Site <- .site_factor(dp$brain_region)
  dp$Property <- les_property_factor(dp$grammatical_property)
  dp$Language <- factor(dp$mini_language, levels = .lang_levels)
  fr9 <- les_erp_frame(min(dp$mean_difference - 1.96 * dp$se_difference),
                       max(dp$mean_difference + 1.96 * dp$se_difference), -3:2)
  blk9 <- function(site)
    ggplot(dp[dp$Site == site, ],
           aes(time, mean_difference, colour = Language, fill = Language)) +
      les_erp_layers(fr9, .next_word_ms) +
      geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean_difference - 1.96 * se_difference,
                      ymax = mean_difference + 1.96 * se_difference),
                  alpha = 0.18, colour = NA) +
      geom_line(linewidth = LES_LWD_TRACE) +
      facet_grid(. ~ Property) +
      les_scale_language() +
      labs(title = site, x = "Time from critical-word onset (ms)",
           y = "Ungrammatical − grammatical (µV)") +
      les_theme()
  .erp_stack(blk9("Midline posterior"), blk9("Left anterior"))
} else {
  les_placeholder("Group difference waves pending the updated extraction")
}
```

### Subject--verb gender agreement

Gender agreement showed the clearest profile. The grammaticality effect was positive in
direction in every window and macroregion ($p_d$ from
`r pd_range("z_recoded_grammaticality", "^erp_gender_agreement", sep = "to")`;
@fig-erp-forest) and credible in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality", "gender_agreement")` cells, all in the two earlier
windows (midline 200--500 ms,
`r report_effect("erp_gender_agreement_200_500_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`;
lateral 300--600 ms,
`r report_effect("erp_gender_agreement_300_600_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`;
midline 300--600 ms,
`r report_effect("erp_gender_agreement_300_600_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`)`r cred_cells_guard("z_recoded_grammaticality", c("erp_gender_agreement_200_500_midline", "erp_gender_agreement_300_600_lateral", "erp_gender_agreement_300_600_midline"), "gender_agreement")`.
Averaged over sessions, the effect was weaker in the late window (midline 400--900 ms,
`r report_effect("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`), but
that is where it grew. The grammaticality $\times$ session interaction was credible in the
late window in both macroregions (lateral,
`r report_effect("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session")`;
midline,
`r report_effect("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session")`)`r cred_cells_guard("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session", c("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_lateral", "erp_gender_agreement_400_900_midline"), "gender_agreement")`
and in neither earlier window (lateral 300--600 ms,
`r report_effect("erp_gender_agreement_300_600_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session")`).
Language modulated neither the effect nor its development. The grammaticality $\times$
language interaction was credible in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language", "gender_agreement")`
gender-agreement cells and the grammaticality $\times$ session $\times$ language
interaction in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language", "gender_agreement")`,
and in the late window, where the effect developed, the latter sat near zero (midline,
`r report_effect("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`).

### Differential object marking

Differential object marking showed an early, transient grammaticality effect (grammatical
trials more positive, a relative violation negativity), and no developing late
effect. The effect was credible in the early window in both macroregions
(@fig-erp-forest; lateral 200--500 ms,
`r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_200_500_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`;
midline,
`r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_200_500_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`)`r cred_cells_guard("z_recoded_grammaticality", c("erp_differential_object_marking_200_500_lateral", "erp_differential_object_marking_200_500_midline"), "differential_object_marking")`,
positive but not credible in the middle window (midline 300--600 ms,
`r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_300_600_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`),
and, if anything, slightly negative by the late window
(midline 400--900 ms, `r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_400_900_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`). One caveat
attaches to this early effect specifically. Because the violation omits the particle
*fi*, the two conditions differ physically in the region preceding the critical word. At
the roughly 505 ms word-onset asynchrony, the response to that region overlaps the
200--500 ms window of the critical epoch. The same low-level difference that renders the
pre-stimulus decoding baseline non-chance (see below) could therefore contribute here, so
we read the early effect as a violation-related response with a possible stimulus-driven
component. The effect did not change credibly across sessions (the grammaticality
$\times$ session interaction was credible in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session", "differential_object_marking")`
cells), and no term involving language was credible (grammaticality $\times$ language,
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language", "differential_object_marking")`;
grammaticality $\times$ session $\times$ language,
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language", "differential_object_marking")`).
The grammaticality $\times$ language interaction came closest in the early lateral window
(`r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_200_500_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language")`),
where it is credible under the simpler random-effect structure (see *Dependence on the
by-item random-effect structure*).

### Verb--object number agreement

Verb--object number agreement, the latest-introduced property, showed no credible term in
any cell (@fig-erp-forest). Its grammaticality effect was small and positive in the early
window and negative in the late one (midline 400--900 ms,
`r report_effect("erp_verb_object_number_agreement_400_900_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`).
The terms involving session leaned positive in the late window without reaching
credibility, both the grammaticality $\times$ session interaction (midline,
`r report_effect("erp_verb_object_number_agreement_400_900_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session")`)
and the grammaticality $\times$ session $\times$ language interaction
(`r report_effect("erp_verb_object_number_agreement_400_900_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`).`r cred_cells_guard("z_recoded_grammaticality", character(0), "verb_object_number_agreement")``r cred_cells_guard("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session", character(0), "verb_object_number_agreement")`

One reading caveat applies to this property alone. Verb--object number agreement is
measured at Sessions 4 and 6 only, and the interval between them is the unrehearsed
retention gap, so for this property the session term is the change across that gap and
contains no further exposure. Its grammaticality $\times$ session and three-way terms are
therefore offline-interval changes, and the *learning* and *language-conditioned development* glosses that the
operationalisation gives those terms for the other two properties do not carry over
unaltered here. We read them accordingly throughout.

### Topography

The models average over the clusters of each macroregion and carry no topographic terms,
so the scalp distribution of the grammaticality effect is described rather than tested.
@fig-erp-topography shows it for each language, property and window.

```{r}
#| label: fig-erp-topography
#| fig-cap: "Scalp Topography of the Grammaticality Effect by Property, Analysis Window and Miniature Language"
#| apa-note: "Maps show the participant-paired ungrammatical-minus-grammatical mean amplitude in each a priori analysis window (column headers, in ms from critical-word onset), baseline-corrected within participant and averaged over each participant's sessions before the group mean. Within each property, the top two rows are the Mini-Norwegian and Mini-English groups and the bottom row, set apart, is their difference (Mini-Norwegian minus Mini-English). Negative values (blue) mark a relative negativity for violations. Each map is a penalised thin-plate spline surface fitted to the 30 electrodes assigned to the analysis regions, at the recorded montage positions (dots; nose at the top), and masked to the head, so no value is shown for scalp the montage did not sample. The two low-temporal sites below the equator, FT9 and FT10 (open circles beside the ears), shape the surface at the rim. The thin dark line is the zero contour. The colour scale is symmetric about zero and shared by every map here and in the session-resolved maps in the appendix on group displays by session. The sample is the one the models are fitted to. The maps are descriptive and are not electrode-wise tests."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: !expr if (group_figures_ready) 2.5 else 1
elec_xy <- .read_csv_if(paper1_results("_electrode_coordinates.csv"))
ediff <- if (group_figures_ready) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(.group_topo_files, utils::read.csv, stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
} else NULL

# Smoothed scalp maps (penalised thin-plate regression spline) for any subset of the
# window-difference table. `ed` carries electrode, diff and the columns named in `keys`;
# every combination of `keys` becomes one map. The head outline is the equator, which the
# montage's projection places at radius 1 (derived from the sensors 90 degrees from the
# vertex rather than assumed). The map is masked to the head, so no value is shown for
# scalp the montage never measured.
.topo_surfaces <- function(ed, keys) {
  R  <- mean(sqrt(elec_xy$x^2 + elec_xy$y^2)[abs(elec_xy$theta) == 90])
  gr <- expand.grid(x = seq(-R, R, length.out = 110), y = seq(-R, R, length.out = 110))
  gr <- gr[sqrt(gr$x^2 + gr$y^2) <= R, ]
  ed <- dplyr::left_join(ed, elec_xy[, c("electrode", "x", "y")], by = "electrode")
  ed <- ed[!is.na(ed$x) & !is.na(ed$diff), ]
  one <- function(dd) {
    m <- tryCatch(mgcv::gam(diff ~ s(x, y, k = 20), data = dd, method = "REML"),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(m)) return(NULL)
    out <- gr
    out$diff <- as.numeric(stats::predict(m, newdata = gr))
    for (k in keys) out[[k]] <- dd[[k]][1]
    out
  }
  surf <- do.call(rbind, Filter(Negate(is.null),
                                lapply(split(ed, interaction(ed[keys], drop = TRUE)), one)))
  list(surf = surf, sensors = ed, R = R)
}

# Display constants, shared with the session-resolved maps in Appendix E. Every map is
# .map_in wide at print size. The frame, in multiples of the head radius R, encloses the
# nose, the ears and the two sensors below the equator (FT9/FT10), so the panels are
# clipped without cutting any of them and no mark strays into a neighbouring map.
.map_in  <- 0.55
.topo_xl <- c(-1.27, 1.27)
.topo_yl <- c(-1.03, 1.14)
.map_asp <- diff(.topo_yl) / diff(.topo_xl)
.win_lab <- c(`200_500` = "200–500", `300_600` = "300–600", `400_900` = "400–900")
.grp_lab <- c(`Mini-Norwegian` = "Mini-Norwegian", `Mini-English` = "Mini-English",
              `Mini-Norwegian - Mini-English` = "Group\ndifference")

# One block of maps. `tp` is a list(surf, sensors, R) restricted to the block; `rows` and
# `cols` name its two facet factors, and `lim` is the colour limit shared by every map of
# this figure and of the session-resolved figure. The block title, the column headers and
# the row labels are switched on only where the assembled figure needs them.
.topo_block <- function(tp, rows, cols, lim, title = NULL, show_rows = TRUE, show_cols = TRUE) {
  R  <- tp$R
  tt <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 240)
  ea <- seq(-pi / 2.6, pi / 2.6, length.out = 60)
  outline <- rbind(
    data.frame(part = "head", x = R * cos(tt), y = R * sin(tt)),
    data.frame(part = "nose", x = c(-0.13, 0, 0.13) * R, y = c(0.985, 1.12, 0.985) * R),
    # Ears, so the two low-temporal sensors outside the outline read as electrodes in an
    # anatomically sensible position rather than as stray marks.
    data.frame(part = "ear_r", x = R * (0.10 * cos(ea) + 0.995), y = 0.19 * R * sin(ea)),
    data.frame(part = "ear_l", x = -R * (0.10 * cos(ea) + 0.995), y = 0.19 * R * sin(ea)))
  # The outline and the sensors go only into the panels that carry a surface, so a map
  # whose smooth failed stays empty and never shows as a blank (flat 0 µV) head.
  panels <- unique(tp$surf[c(rows, cols)])
  outline <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(panels)), function(i)
    cbind(outline, panels[i, , drop = FALSE], row.names = NULL)))
  key <- function(d) paste(d[[rows]], d[[cols]])
  s <- tp$sensors[key(tp$sensors) %in% key(panels), ]
  inside <- sqrt(s$x^2 + s$y^2) <= R + 1e-9
  n_rows <- length(unique(panels[[rows]]))
  n_cols <- length(unique(panels[[cols]]))
  ggplot(tp$surf, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_raster(aes(fill = diff), interpolate = TRUE) +
    # The zero contour carries the sign of the difference as a second cue, so a map
    # survives greyscale printing.
    geom_contour(aes(z = diff), breaks = 0, colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.25) +
    geom_path(data = outline, aes(x, y, group = part), colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_point(data = s[inside, ], aes(x, y), size = 0.4, stroke = 0, colour = "grey10") +
    geom_point(data = s[!inside, ], aes(x, y), shape = 1, size = 0.7, stroke = 0.3,
               colour = "grey10") +
    facet_grid(stats::reformulate(cols, rows), switch = "y") +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = les_div[1], mid = les_div[2], high = les_div[3], midpoint = 0,
                         limits = c(-lim, lim), breaks = scales::breaks_width(1),
                         oob = scales::oob_squish, labels = les_lab_num,
                         name = "Ungrammatical − grammatical (µV)") +
    coord_fixed(xlim = .topo_xl * R, ylim = .topo_yl * R, expand = FALSE, clip = "on") +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme_void(base_size = LES_FIG_BASE_SIZE - 2) +
    # Every label is 8 pt at print size. The maps are fixed at .map_in, so blocks of
    # different widths keep one map size; 4 pt between maps keeps each header and each
    # pair of FT9/FT10 circles with its own map. The colour bar is 5 key widths long
    # (2.25 in).
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5, vjust = 0,
                                    lineheight = 0.95, margin = margin(b = 3)),
          strip.text.x = if (show_cols) element_text(size = 8, margin = margin(b = 2)) else
            element_blank(),
          strip.text.y.left = if (show_rows) element_text(size = 8, angle = 0, hjust = 1,
                                                          lineheight = 0.95,
                                                          margin = margin(r = 4)) else
            element_blank(),
          strip.placement = "outside",
          panel.spacing = unit(4, "pt"),
          panel.widths = unit(rep(.map_in, n_cols), "in"),
          panel.heights = unit(rep(.map_in * .map_asp, n_rows), "in"),
          legend.position = "bottom",
          legend.title.position = "top",
          legend.title = element_text(size = 8, hjust = 0.5),
          legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
          legend.key.width = unit(0.45, "in"),
          legend.key.height = unit(0.1, "in"),
          legend.ticks = element_line(colour = "grey15", linewidth = 0.3),
          legend.margin = margin(t = 4),
          plot.margin = margin(1, 3, 1, 3))
}
# A block's share of a list(surf, sensors, R).
.topo_subset <- function(tp, keep) list(surf = tp$surf[keep(tp$surf), , drop = FALSE],
                                        sensors = tp$sensors[keep(tp$sensors), , drop = FALSE],
                                        R = tp$R)

tp <- ts <- NULL
if (!is.null(ediff) && !is.null(elec_xy) && requireNamespace("mgcv", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ep <- ediff[ediff$session == "pooled", ]
  # The group difference is a between-participant contrast of two independent means.
  gd <- merge(ep[ep$mini_language == "Mini-Norwegian", c("grammatical_property", "electrode", "window", "mean_difference")],
              ep[ep$mini_language == "Mini-English",   c("grammatical_property", "electrode", "window", "mean_difference")],
              by = c("grammatical_property", "electrode", "window"), suffixes = c("_n", "_e"))
  gd$mean_difference <- gd$mean_difference_n - gd$mean_difference_e
  gd$mini_language <- "Mini-Norwegian - Mini-English"
  ed <- rbind(ep[, c("grammatical_property", "electrode", "window", "mini_language", "mean_difference")],
              gd[, c("grammatical_property", "electrode", "window", "mini_language", "mean_difference")])
  ed$diff <- ed$mean_difference
  tp <- .topo_surfaces(ed, c("grammatical_property", "window", "mini_language"))
  # The session-resolved late-window surfaces of Appendix E are estimated here as well, so
  # that one colour limit, rounded up to 0.5 µV, covers every map of both figures and a
  # colour means the same voltage in each.
  es <- ediff[ediff$session != "pooled" & ediff$window == "400_900", ]
  es$diff <- es$mean_difference
  ts <- .topo_surfaces(es, c("grammatical_property", "session", "mini_language"))
  .topo_lim <- ceiling(2 * max(abs(c(tp$surf$diff, ts$surf$diff)), na.rm = TRUE)) / 2
  if (!is.finite(.topo_lim) || .topo_lim == 0) .topo_lim <- 1
  for (nm in c("surf", "sensors")) {
    tp[[nm]]$Property <- les_property_factor(tp[[nm]]$grammatical_property)
    tp[[nm]]$Window   <- factor(unname(.win_lab[tp[[nm]]$window]), levels = .win_lab)
    tp[[nm]]$Group    <- factor(unname(.grp_lab[tp[[nm]]$mini_language]), levels = .grp_lab)
  }
  # Sensors are drawn once per map.
  tp$sensors <- tp$sensors[!duplicated(tp$sensors[c("Property", "Window", "Group", "electrode")]), ]
  # Three property blocks side by side: the two groups above, and their difference, a
  # different quantity, in a row of its own set further down. Window headers go on the
  # top blocks and group labels left of the first block only.
  .diff_lab <- .grp_lab[["Mini-Norwegian - Mini-English"]]
  .tp_props <- levels(droplevels(tp$surf$Property))
  .topo_top <- lapply(seq_along(.tp_props), function(i)
    .topo_block(.topo_subset(tp, function(d) d$Property == .tp_props[i] & d$Group != .diff_lab),
                "Group", "Window", .topo_lim, title = .tp_props[i], show_rows = i == 1))
  .topo_bot <- lapply(seq_along(.tp_props), function(i)
    .topo_block(.topo_subset(tp, function(d) d$Property == .tp_props[i] & d$Group == .diff_lab),
                "Group", "Window", .topo_lim, show_rows = i == 1, show_cols = FALSE) +
      theme(plot.margin = margin(8, 3, 1, 3)))
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(patchwork))
  patchwork::wrap_plots(c(.topo_top, .topo_bot), ncol = length(.tp_props), byrow = TRUE,
                        guides = "collect") &
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
} else {
  les_placeholder("Group-separated scalp topography pending the updated per-electrode extraction")
}
```

### Dependence on the by-item random-effect structure

Everything above comes from the maximal structure, with crossed by-participant and
by-item random effects each carrying a grammaticality slope. Refitting the whole grid
without the by-item grammaticality slope changes almost nothing. At the median, the
grammaticality main effect's intervals under the maximal structure are
`r itemslope_width_ratio("z_recoded_grammaticality")` times their width without the slope,
and the same cells are credible under both structures for every grammaticality term but
one. That one is the grammaticality $\times$ language interaction for differential object
marking in the early lateral window, credible without the by-item slope
(`r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_200_500_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language", exact = TRUE)`)
and just short of credibility with it, as reported
above.`r cred_agree_guard("", "_itemslope", differ = "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language")`
No conclusion here rests on that cell. The comparison is set out in full in
@apx-analytic-decisions-in-detail.

## Retention (Session 4 to Session 6)

The retention contrast quantifies the change in the grammaticality effect between Sessions
4 and 6, positive values indicating an effect that strengthened over the interval and
values near zero an effect that held steady. Its derivation bounds what it can show. Session
enters the models as a single linear predictor, so the contrast is the per-session change
in the grammaticality effect rescaled to the width of the retention step. Every session in
the series informs that estimate, including those outside the retention interval. For
gender agreement, sampled from Session 2, and for differential object marking, sampled
from Session 3, the contrast describes the fitted trajectory evaluated over the retention
interval. It cannot by itself separate an offline gain specific to that interval
from continued improvement at the rate the training sessions established. Verb--object
number agreement is the exception, being present at Sessions 4 and 6 only, so for that
property the linear session term is precisely the change across those two sessions and the
contrast is estimated directly from them. @tbl-retention, in @apx-retention-tables,
reports every contrast overall, within each language and, where derived, as the
between-language difference; the text below reports the ones that carry the argument.

For gender agreement and differential object marking, that limitation is addressed
directly. Both properties were refitted with an indicator for the retention session,
interacted with grammaticality and language, so that the linear term carries the training
trend and the indicator the deviation at Session 6. @tbl-retention-free, in the same
appendix, reports those freed contrasts. They answer a different question from @tbl-retention, and where the two
disagree, the freed estimate is the one that bears on consolidation. Verb--object number
agreement admits no such refit, for the reason given under *Model structure*.

A retention contrast was credible for gender agreement alone, in the late window where its
development across sessions was also credible. There the grammaticality effect strengthened
across the interval in both macroregions (lateral 400--900 ms,
`r report_contrast("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_lateral", "overall")`; midline,
`r report_contrast("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_midline", "overall")`)`r ret_cred_guard("overall", c("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_lateral", "erp_gender_agreement_400_900_midline"))`.
Within the groups, the strengthening was credible for Mini-English in the lateral cell
(`r report_contrast("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_lateral", "within_Mini-English")`) and for
neither group elsewhere`r ret_cred_guard("within_Mini-English", "erp_gender_agreement_400_900_lateral")``r ret_cred_guard("within_Mini-Norwegian", character(0))`,
and the difference between the groups was not credible in any cell (lateral,
`r report_contrast("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_lateral", "language_difference")`)`r ret_cred_guard("language_difference", character(0))`.
A credible change in one group and not in the other is not evidence that the groups differ
[@gelmanstern2006; @nieuwenhuis2011], so we read the gender-agreement result as a
strengthening common to both. No retention contrast was credible for differential object
marking or for verb--object number agreement (@tbl-retention). For verb--object number
agreement, whose session term is itself the change across the interval, the late-window
contrast leaned positive in the Mini-Norwegian group without reaching credibility (midline
400--900 ms,
`r report_contrast("erp_verb_object_number_agreement_400_900_midline", "within_Mini-Norwegian")`).

The refits that free the Session 6 step qualify the gender-agreement result. In them, the
deviation of the Session 6 effect from the training trend was credible in
`r retfree_tally("gender_agreement", "overall", "credible")` gender-agreement cells, and the
difference between the groups in that deviation in
`r retfree_tally("gender_agreement", "language_difference", "credible")` (midline
400--900 ms, `r retfree_val("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_midline")`;
`r ret_lang_diff(freed = TRUE)`)`r ret_cred_guard("overall", character(0), freed = TRUE)`. The freed deviation is estimated far less precisely than
the linear contrast, so it cannot tell whether the late-window effect went on growing over
the interval at the training rate, held or fell back somewhat. What it shows is that the
Session 6 effect did not depart credibly from the trend the training sessions set. For
differential object marking, the freed deviation was credible overall in
`r retfree_tally("differential_object_marking", "overall", "credible")` cells, but in the
Mini-Norwegian group the Session 6 effect fell credibly below its training trend in the two
early midline cells (200--500 ms,
`r retfree_val("erp_differential_object_marking_200_500_midline", "within_Mini-Norwegian")`;
300--600 ms,
`r retfree_val("erp_differential_object_marking_300_600_midline", "within_Mini-Norwegian")`),
and the difference between the groups was credible in the same
cells (`r retfree_val("erp_differential_object_marking_200_500_midline", "language_difference")`;
`r retfree_val("erp_differential_object_marking_300_600_midline", "language_difference")`)`r ret_cred_guard("within_Mini-Norwegian", c("erp_differential_object_marking_200_500_midline", "erp_differential_object_marking_300_600_midline"), freed = TRUE)``r ret_cred_guard("language_difference", c("erp_differential_object_marking_200_500_midline", "erp_differential_object_marking_300_600_midline"), freed = TRUE)``r ret_cred_guard("within_Mini-English", character(0), freed = TRUE)`.
For this property, the training trend rests on two sessions a week apart, so the projection
the deviation is measured from is itself uncertain, and the early window carries the possible
stimulus-driven component described above. Without the reprocessed and recovered records,
every contrast credible in the primary analysis remains credible with the same sign, and one
further contrast becomes credible, the late midline gender-agreement strengthening within
Mini-English, which under the protocol cannot become a claim
(@tbl-retention-robustness).`r ret_robust_guard(extra = "erp_gender_agreement_400_900_midline within_Mini-English")`

## Grammaticality judgements

Accuracy on grammatical and on ungrammatical sentences reflects two separable quantities
(see *Signal-detection reading of the judgement models*). Sensitivity is how well a
learner told the two sentence types apart. The criterion is how readily they judged a
sentence grammatical, whichever type it was. @fig-sdt-by-language shows both for each
group, and the accuracies they are computed from are given in @fig-accuracy-by-language.`r acc_rt_switch_marker()`

```{r}
#| label: fig-sdt-by-language
#| fig-cap: "Sensitivity and Criterion in the Grammaticality Judgements by Miniature Language, Property and Session"
#| apa-note: "Points are group means of participant-level $d'$ (upper row) and criterion $c$ (lower row), computed from each participant's hit rate (answering grammatical to a grammatical sentence) and false-alarm rate (answering grammatical to an ungrammatical one) at each session, with the log-linear correction for extreme rates. The horizontal line marks zero, which is chance-level sensitivity in the upper row and an unbiased criterion in the lower row, where a negative value is a readiness to judge sentences grammatical. Vertical lines are 95% *t* intervals over participants, and every participant receives equal weight. Each property is plotted from the session at which it entered the design: gender agreement at Session 2, differential object marking at Session 3 and verb--object number agreement at Session 4. These are descriptive, probit-scale summaries; the inferential estimates in the text come from the trial-level models, whose logit-scale sensitivity is about 1.7 times $d'$. Sessions are equally spaced, as in the models, although Sessions 2 to 4 are a week apart and Session 6 follows about four months without exposure."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: !expr if (group_figures_ready) 4.6 else 1
if (group_figures_ready && !is.null(sdt_desc_tbl)) {
  # Shared behavioural encoding (Figure E3, Paper 2's trajectory figure): Session is a
  # factor, so sessions are equally spaced as in the models, and free_x drops the sessions
  # before a property entered the design instead of drawing them empty.
  sdd <- les_judgement_frame(sdt_desc_tbl)
  stopifnot(!anyNA(sdd$Property))
  # The measure strips replace the y-axis title (les_row_title_theme()); plotmath gives
  # the italic d with a true prime and the italic c.
  sdd$Measure <- factor(sdd$measure, levels = c("d_prime", "criterion"),
                        labels = c('"Sensitivity ("*italic(d)*"′)"',
                                   '"Criterion ("*italic(c)*")"'))
  ggplot(sdd, aes(Session, mean_value, colour = Language, shape = Language, group = Language)) +
    les_ref_h(0) +
    les_judgement_layers() +
    facet_grid(Measure ~ Property, scales = "free", space = "free_x", switch = "y",
               labeller = labeller(Measure = label_parsed, Property = les_wrap(18))) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = les_lab_num) +
    les_scale_language() + les_scale_language_shape() +
    labs(x = "Session") +
    les_judgement_theme() + les_row_title_theme() +
    # Property labels share a baseline just above their panels, one line or two.
    theme(strip.text.x = element_text(vjust = 0))
} else {
  les_placeholder("Signal-detection summaries pending the updated extraction")
}
```

Sensitivity was high at each property's first session and declined from there in both
groups (@tbl-sdt-contrasts). Between Sessions 2 and 6, sensitivity to gender agreement fell
in the Mini-Norwegian group
(`r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "sensitivity", "change_first_to_last", "2->6", "Mini-Norwegian")`)
and in the Mini-English group
(`r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "sensitivity", "change_first_to_last", "2->6", "Mini-English")`).
The declines for differential object marking were larger, and the one change that was not
credible was that of the Mini-English group for verb--object number agreement
(`r report_sdt("verb_object_number_agreement", "sensitivity", "change_first_to_last", "4->6", "Mini-English")`).
The decline runs against the improvement that motivated the positive prior on the session
term. Two features of the design bear on it. Properties accumulate, so a judgement made at
Session 4 is made against a grammar with three manipulated properties instead of one, and
Session 6 follows about four months without exposure. The design has no condition that holds
task demands constant while sessions advance, so we do not separate these two sources of
decline.

A group difference in sensitivity was credible `r sdt_language_clause("sensitivity")`. For
gender agreement, the only property with a Norwegian analogue, the difference between the
groups averaged over sessions was
`r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "sensitivity", "language_difference", "average")`
(Mini-Norwegian minus Mini-English), and at the retention session it was
`r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "sensitivity", "language_difference", "6")`. The
Mini-Norwegian estimate was the lower of the two at every session.`r sdt_claims_guard()`

In the reported models, the groups diverged more clearly in their criterion. The difference
between the groups' criteria was credible `r sdt_language_clause("criterion")`. For gender agreement, the Mini-Norwegian
group's criterion became more liberal between Sessions 2 and 6
(`r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "criterion", "change_first_to_last", "2->6", "Mini-Norwegian")`),
whereas the Mini-English group's did not change credibly
(`r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "criterion", "change_first_to_last", "2->6", "Mini-English")`).
At retention, the difference between the groups was
`r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "criterion", "language_difference", "6")`, and the difference
in how far the criterion moved between the first and last sessions was
`r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "criterion", "change_first_to_last_language_difference", "2->6")`.
At `r sdt_credible_sessions("gender_agreement", "criterion")`, then, Mini-Norwegian learners
judged gender-agreement sentences grammatical more readily than Mini-English learners did,
ungrammatical ones included, without telling the two types apart any better. For differential object marking, the
criterion became more conservative in both groups (Mini-Norwegian
`r report_sdt("differential_object_marking", "criterion", "change_first_to_last", "3->6", "Mini-Norwegian")`;
Mini-English
`r report_sdt("differential_object_marking", "criterion", "change_first_to_last", "3->6", "Mini-English")`),
and for verb--object number agreement it did not change credibly in either.

In the fitted models, the gender-agreement criterion difference is carried by the
grammaticality $\times$ language and grammaticality $\times$ session $\times$ language terms
(`r report_effect("accuracy_gender_agreement", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language")`;
`r report_effect("accuracy_gender_agreement", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`),
and the sensitivity difference by the language and session $\times$ language terms
(`r report_effect("accuracy_gender_agreement", "z_recoded_mini_language")`;
`r report_effect("accuracy_gender_agreement", "z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`).
The reported models carry by-participant slopes for grammaticality and for session but not
for their interaction, which is the within-participant change in criterion. Refitted with
that slope, the estimates of the difference between the gender-agreement groups' criteria
moved by no more than `r crit_maxranef_shift()` on the logit scale, but their intervals
widened, and the difference was credible
`r sdt_language_clause_model("criterion", "_maxranef")`. At retention it was
`r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "criterion", "language_difference", "6", model = "accuracy_gender_agreement_maxranef")`,
and averaged over sessions it was
