`r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "criterion", "language_difference", "average", model = "accuracy_gender_agreement_maxranef")`.
The difference in how far the criterion moved between Sessions 2 and 6 was not credible in
the refit either
(`r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "criterion", "change_first_to_last_language_difference", "2->6", model = "accuracy_gender_agreement_maxranef")`).
We therefore grade the criterion difference as suggestive (see *Strength of
evidence*).`r maxranef_claims_guard()` `r byitem_sentence()`

For differential object marking, sensitivity declined less in the Mini-Norwegian group than
in the Mini-English group between Sessions 3 and 6
(`r report_sdt("differential_object_marking", "sensitivity", "change_first_to_last_language_difference", "3->6")`).
`r dom_edge_clause()``r dom_sens_guard()`
Differential object marking is absent from both prior languages, so no account predicts
this difference, and we treat it with the other unpredicted control-property effects in the
Discussion.

We also fitted the accuracy models with the reaction-time screen of the project's earlier
preprocessing, which we do not apply (see *Grammaticality-judgement task*).
`r rt_screen_sentence()`

## Multivariate decoding of grammaticality

We decoded
Grammatical from Ungrammatical trials at each time sample (leave-one-participant-out
AUC; @fig-decoding). Error was controlled across time within each analysis by
cluster-based permutation and, within each property, across the clusters of its pooled
overall time-course by Benjamini--Hochberg FDR (the confirmatory correction family; see
*Transparency, preregistration and analysis status*). A significant
cluster licenses only that the grammaticality time-course as a whole departs from
chance. The temporal boundaries of a surviving cluster are not themselves inferential
claims about the onset, offset or duration of the effect [@sassenhagen2019cluster], and
we do not read them as such.`r decode_status_results()`
<!-- STATUS (10 October 2026): every value in this section comes from the decoding rerun on
     the corrected sample (HTC 8960051-8960055, cross-property 9013904). The confirmatory
     time-courses are final at B = 1,000. Verb-object number agreement's run finished; the
     time-courses of gender agreement and differential object marking were assembled from
     their banked pooled blocks by scripts/09b_assemble_confirmatory_timecourse.R (HTC
     9029773) while their runs complete the secondary analyses, which decode_runs_pending()
     discloses in rendered prose until their cross-language files land. The second correction
     layer is kept as specified, and the clusters that pass the maximum-cluster test are
     reported beside it (ISSUES.md G08-05, decided 10 October 2026). -->

```{r}
#| label: fig-decoding
#| fig-cap: "Time-Resolved Decoding of Grammaticality for Each Property"
#| apa-note: "Lines are leave-one-participant-out decoding AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) for grammatical against ungrammatical trials at each 4-ms sample, all sessions pooled (the confirmatory analysis). The solid grey horizontal line marks chance (AUC = 0.5) and the dashed line the cluster-forming threshold, the 95th percentile of the pooled within-participant permutation null. Black bars below each time-course mark the extent of the clusters that survive Benjamini--Hochberg false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction (*q* < .05) across the clusters of that property's time-course, and the text in each panel gives their number and adjusted cluster-level *p* values (*q*). Grey bars mark clusters that pass the maximum-cluster permutation test (*p* < .05), which controls the family-wise error rate across time, but not the second, FDR layer. A bar marks cluster membership, not sample-by-sample significance, and its edges are not estimates of onset or offset. The vertical grey line marks critical-word onset (0 ms), and the shaded interval before it is a negative control, in which decoding should sit at chance. The AUC is a point estimate: the pipeline records no per-fold dispersion, so no uncertainty band is drawn. All panels share one vertical scale."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: !expr local({n <- sum(vapply(decode_tc, function(d) !is.null(d) && any(d$analysis == "overall", na.rm = TRUE), logical(1))); if (n) 1.3 + 1.3 * n else 1})
# The height counts the properties with an overall time-course: 1.3 in per panel plus
# 1.3 in of legend, axis and strips, so 5.2 in for all three, and 1 in for the
# placeholder. A property whose time-course has not landed yet gets no panel at all
# (decode_ready allows partial availability, and gender agreement's rerun follows the
# other two).
ov <- NULL
if (decode_ready) {
  # The confirmatory analysis only: each property's pooled overall time-course.
  ov <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(.decode_props), function(p) {
    d <- decode_tc[[p]]; if (is.null(d)) return(NULL)
    o <- d[d$analysis == "overall", , drop = FALSE]
    if (!nrow(o)) return(NULL)
    o$Property <- p; o
  }))
}
if (!is.null(ov) && nrow(ov)) {
  # droplevels(): les_property_factor() carries all three property levels, and the label
  # and reference-line frames below are built over levels(ov$Property). An absent
  # property must not get a panel, least of all one reading "No cluster survives".
  ov$Property <- droplevels(les_property_factor(ov$Property))
  # Surviving clusters as intervals, not per-sample points: a cluster test licenses
  # cluster membership, not sample-by-sample significance. Each bar is widened by half a
  # 4-ms sample at either end, so a one-sample cluster still has a visible extent.
  cl <- ov[ov$significant_fdr %in% c(TRUE, "TRUE") & !is.na(ov$cluster_id), , drop = FALSE]
  # With no surviving cluster in any panel, summarise() would evaluate min() on an empty
  # slice and warn, so that case gets an empty frame of the same shape.
  cl <- if (nrow(cl)) dplyr::summarise(dplyr::group_by(cl, Property, cluster_id),
                                       x = min(time_ms) - 2, xend = max(time_ms) + 2,
                                       q = dplyr::first(cluster_p_fdr), .groups = "drop") else
    data.frame(Property = ov$Property[0], cluster_id = cl$cluster_id, x = numeric(),
               xend = numeric(), q = numeric())
  # Clusters that pass the maximum-cluster test but not the second layer, drawn in grey, so
  # that the figure shows what each layer leaves as the text does (see the appendix on the
  # decoding correction family).
  cfw <- ov[!is.na(ov$cluster_id) & !is.na(ov$cluster_p) & ov$cluster_p < .05 &
              !(ov$significant_fdr %in% c(TRUE, "TRUE")), , drop = FALSE]
  cfw <- if (nrow(cfw)) dplyr::summarise(dplyr::group_by(cfw, Property, cluster_id),
                                         x = min(time_ms) - 2, xend = max(time_ms) + 2,
                                         .groups = "drop") else
    data.frame(Property = ov$Property[0], cluster_id = cfw$cluster_id, x = numeric(),
               xend = numeric())
  # One summary label per panel (the number of surviving clusters and the range of their
  # q values) in place of one label per bar, which overprinted where clusters sit close
  # together. q is printed to three decimals like the p values in the text.
  .q_txt <- function(q) {
    s <- sub("^0", "", formatC(q, format = "f", digits = 3))
    ifelse(s == ".000", "< .001", paste("=", s))
  }
  lab <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(levels(ov$Property), function(pr) {
    k <- cl[cl$Property == pr, , drop = FALSE]
    nfw <- sum(cfw$Property == pr)
    txt <- if (!nrow(k)) {
      if (nfw) sprintf("'No cluster survives FDR correction (%d %s the maximum-cluster test)'",
                       nfw, if (nfw == 1L) "passes" else "pass") else
        "'No cluster survives FDR correction'"
    } else {
      r  <- .q_txt(range(k$q))
      # "q < .001–.035" would read as a bound on a range, so a range whose lower end
      # rounds to .000 is written out ("q from < .001 to .035").
      qs <- if (r[1] == r[2]) r[1] else if (startsWith(r[1], "<"))
        paste("from", r[1], "to", sub("^= ", "", r[2])) else
        paste0(r[1], "–", sub("^= ", "", r[2]))
      sprintf("'%d %s FDR correction,'~italic(q)~'%s'", nrow(k),
              if (nrow(k) == 1L) "cluster survives" else "clusters survive", qs)
    }
    data.frame(Property = factor(pr, levels = levels(ov$Property)), txt = txt)
  }))
  # Chance and the cluster-forming threshold as one keyed layer: the linetype, colour and
  # width scales share their name and breaks, so ggplot2 merges them into one legend whose
  # keys match the lines.
  thr  <- dplyr::distinct(ov, Property, cluster_threshold)
  refs <- rbind(data.frame(Property = factor(levels(ov$Property), levels(ov$Property)),
                           y = 0.5, k = "Chance"),
                data.frame(Property = thr$Property, y = thr$cluster_threshold,
                           k = "Cluster-forming threshold"))
  # Bars in a strip just below the lowest AUC of any panel, and headroom above the highest
  # for the label; one vertical scale for every panel.
  ybar  <- min(ov$auc, na.rm = TRUE) - 0.008
  ylims <- c(ybar - 0.006, max(ov$auc, na.rm = TRUE) + 0.024)
  # Take the floor down to the next 0.05 break when that costs little, so a labelled tick
  # sits below the lowest trace and the bars. The extra 0.001 keeps that break inside the
  # limits, where floating point could otherwise censor it.
  .ylo <- floor(ylims[1] / 0.05) * 0.05
  if (ylims[1] - .ylo < 0.015) ylims[1] <- .ylo - 0.001
  ggplot(ov, aes(time_ms, auc)) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = 0, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = LES_PRESTIM_FILL) +
    les_ref_v(0) +
    geom_hline(data = refs, aes(yintercept = y, linetype = k, colour = k, linewidth = k)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = LES_LWD_TRACE, colour = "black") +
    geom_segment(data = cfw, aes(x = x, xend = xend, y = ybar, yend = ybar),
                 inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "grey65", linewidth = 1.6, lineend = "butt") +
    geom_segment(data = cl, aes(x = x, xend = xend, y = ybar, yend = ybar),
                 inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 1.6, lineend = "butt") +
    # vjust a little above 1 keeps the ascenders clear of the panel's clipping edge.
    geom_text(data = lab, aes(label = txt), x = 1096, y = ylims[2], parse = TRUE,
              inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = 1, vjust = 1.25, size = LES_TEXT_PT / .pt,
              colour = LES_INK) +
    facet_wrap(~ Property, ncol = 1) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Chance = "solid", `Cluster-forming threshold` = "42"),
                          name = NULL) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(Chance = LES_REF_COL, `Cluster-forming threshold` = "grey40"),
                        name = NULL) +
    scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(Chance = LES_LWD_REF, `Cluster-forming threshold` = 0.35),
                           name = NULL) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1000, 200), expand = c(0, 0)) +
    # AUC keeps its leading zero, as in the text.
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_width(0.05),
                       labels = scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.01)) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-100, 1100), ylim = ylims, expand = FALSE) +
    labs(x = "Time from critical-word onset (ms)", y = "Decoding AUC") +
    les_theme(grid = "y") +
    # Wide enough for the dashed key to show its pattern.
    theme(legend.key.width = unit(22, "pt"))
} else {
  # A placeholder figure rather than text, so the cross-references to this figure resolve
  # in a draft rendered without the decoding artefacts.
  les_placeholder("Decoding time-courses withheld pending the rerun")
}
```

The three properties differed here too, though the ordering of their raw separability has
to be read against the pre-stimulus baseline.
Differential object marking, whose univariate signature was the weakest and
shortest-lived, was by far the most separable, though not necessarily by a violation
response: its overall time-course carried
`r dec_count(dec_dom, "n_overall_fdr", "cluster")` surviving FDR correction, peaking post-stimulus at AUC
`r dec_val(dec_dom, "max_auc_ov", 2)` (at `r dec_val(dec_dom, "peak_ms")` ms;
@fig-decoding). The pre-stimulus baseline should sit at chance. For the other properties,
no cluster reaching into it passed the maximum-cluster
test`r dec_prestim_guard("gender_agreement")``r dec_prestim_guard("verb_object_number_agreement")`,
but differential object marking's pre-stimulus AUC averaged
`r dec_val(dec_dom, "pre_mean_auc", 2)` with
`r dec_count(dec_dom, "pre_n_fdr", "sample")` surviving FDR before the critical word. Its
highest AUC anywhere in the epoch falls in that baseline
(`r dec_val(dec_dom, "pre_max_auc", 2)`), above its post-stimulus peak.
Part of the differential-object-marking separability therefore precedes the stimulus
and may reflect a low-level difference between conditions, for instance the physical
presence of the object marker in the preceding region, and need not reflect a violation
response. Peak AUCs are quoted on the post-stimulus axis for this reason. The extents
of the surviving clusters make the limit concrete: one lies wholly before the critical
word (`r dec_span("differential_object_marking", 1)`) and the other begins just before
onset and spans the epoch (`r dec_span("differential_object_marking", 2)`). The
cluster test cannot attribute any part of the surviving separability specifically to a
violation response. What it establishes is that the conditions are separable throughout
the trial. Nor does the pre-stimulus level bound how much that difference contributes after
onset, because the response to the preceding word continues into the epoch and need not keep
its pre-stimulus strength or pattern there.`r if (.decode_run_done("differential_object_marking")) dec_tgm_sentence("differential_object_marking") else ""`
Gender agreement, whose amplitude effect was credible in the region-averaged models,
produced `r dec_count(dec_gender, "n_overall_fdr", "cluster")` in its pooled time-course
surviving the confirmatory correction (@fig-decoding).`r dec_layers_sentence(dec_gender, "gender_agreement")`
It peaked post-stimulus at AUC `r dec_val(dec_gender, "max_auc_ov", 2)` (at
`r dec_val(dec_gender, "peak_ms")` ms). Its pre-stimulus baseline sat at
chance`r dec_prestim_guard("gender_agreement")`, so, unlike differential object marking, it
carries no separability that precedes the critical word, and none of its clusters can be
attributed to a difference in the region before it. Verb--object number agreement produced
`r dec_count(dec_verb, "n_overall_fdr", "cluster")` surviving correction in its pooled
time-course (smallest cluster-level `r dec_min_p(dec_verb)` across all its analyses,
before or after correction, and peak overall AUC
`r dec_val(dec_verb, "max_auc_ov", 2)`).`r dec_robust_sentence()` Cross-language generalisation, in which the
decoder is trained on one mini-language and tested on the other, peaked post-stimulus at
AUC `r dec_val(dec_gender, "max_auc_xlang", 2)` for gender agreement,
`r dec_val(dec_dom, "max_auc_xlang", 2)` for differential object marking and
`r dec_val(dec_verb, "max_auc_xlang", 2)` for verb--object number agreement. Those
values`r if (.decode_run_done("differential_object_marking")) ", and the temporal-generalisation ones," else ""` are descriptive. The generalisation AUCs are
computed over test trials pooled across participants, so, unlike the time-course AUC, they
can be moved by differences between participants in class balance or in their overall
classifier scores. No permutation null was
computed for them, so we treat them as converging context and do not read the transfer
question off them.
Cross-property generalisation stayed close to chance (peak post-stimulus AUC
`r xprop_max()` across all six train--test pairs, reached when a decoder trained on
`r xprop_max_pair()`). This too is descriptive. It has
no permutation null, and because every participant contributes trials to all
three properties, the train and test sets are not participant-independent. Its
theoretical reading is taken up in the Discussion. Because each per-cell decoding
score is a mean cross-validated AUC estimated on cells of differing and sometimes
small participant numbers, the
ordering across properties is provisional, and every cluster-level decision reported here
rests on the well-populated pooled time-course [@varoquaux2018].

# Discussion

Two groups of Norwegian--English bilinguals learned miniature languages that shared their
grammatical morphemes but differed in lexicon and in where gender was marked. For gender
agreement, the one property Norwegian has and English lacks, the Mini-Norwegian group was
not more sensitive than the Mini-English group. In the judgements, `r sens_gender_clause()`.
In the ERP response, the grammaticality $\times$ language term was credible
in `r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language", "gender_agreement")`
gender-agreement cells (@fig-erp-forest, second row), and its development across sessions, the grammaticality $\times$
session $\times$ language term, in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language", "gender_agreement")`.
In the reported models, the groups differed more clearly in their response criterion. In the
later sessions, Mini-Norwegian learners judged gender-agreement sentences grammatical more
readily than Mini-English learners did, ungrammatical ones included, although that difference
was not credible once each learner's change in criterion was modelled, and we grade it as
suggestive. Neither control property showed a
credible group difference in sensitivity, and no ERP grammaticality
effect, or change in one across the training sessions, was credibly modulated by language. We
take these findings in turn, beginning with what they imply for the transfer accounts.

## Gender agreement and the transfer accounts

The Typological Primacy Model predicted that the Norwegian lexicon would lead Mini-Norwegian
learners to Norwegian grammar, gender included, and the English lexicon would lead
Mini-English learners to English, with no gender to draw on [@rothman2015;
@rothmanalemanbanon2015]. Sensitivity to gender agreement should then have been greater in
the Mini-Norwegian group, at least at the earliest sessions. It was not. At Session 2, the
first measurement, the difference in sensitivity between the groups was
`r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "sensitivity", "language_difference", "2")` (Mini-Norwegian
minus Mini-English), and the posterior probability that the Mini-Norwegian group was the more
sensitive was `r sdt_prob_mn_higher("gender_agreement", "sensitivity", "2")`. Averaged over
sessions, that probability was
`r sdt_prob_mn_higher("gender_agreement", "sensitivity", "average")`. The ERP evidence is
consistent with this but less informative. The grammaticality $\times$ language term for gender
agreement was not credible in any window, but its intervals are wide relative to the
grammaticality effect itself, so the ERP data do not exclude a language difference as large
as the effect they measure. The grammaticality effect was credible in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality", "gender_agreement")` cells, so the absence of a
credible language difference is not an absence of any response to measure, but it is not
evidence that the groups responded alike.

Property-by-property accounts allow exactly this outcome. On those accounts, Norwegian
gender is available to every participant, and a learner of either miniature language can
recruit it once the input shows the property to be shared [@westergaard2017;
@westergaard2021]. Their allowance for early lexical influence, and the structural
resemblance of the Mini-Norwegian determiner to its Norwegian counterpart, meant that they
could also have accommodated a Mini-Norwegian advantage. They did not require one, and none
appeared. The data therefore fit property-level availability better than lexically cued
selection of a whole grammar, which is the reading of the design's central contrast that
the accounts' own predictions support.

Three limits apply to that reading, and they are properties of the design, not of the
analysis. The first is that no measurement precedes training. Both groups were already highly
sensitive to gender agreement at Session 2, after pretraining, training and a test, so a
difference in the initial grammar that a single training session erased would leave no
trace here. The Typological Primacy Model expects non-facilitative transfer to be overcome
with input, so these data speak against an advantage that persists into learning more than
against a difference at the very first encounter [@gonzalezalonso2017;
@gonzalezalonso2025]. The second is that no group lacks gender in its first language. High
sensitivity in both groups is what facilitation from Norwegian would produce, but it is also
what learning a salient agreement pattern within a session would produce without any
transfer, so the design cannot show that Norwegian helped either group. For the same reason,
it cannot rule out the L2 Status Factor, which also predicts no Mini-Norwegian advantage. The
third is that sensitivity in a judgement and the amplitude of a violation response index
processing. Neither establishes the grammar that supports it, and the learners' responses
may rest on more than linguistic computation [@gonzalezalonso2020]. The design was not built
to settle the transfer debate, and these findings narrow it only as far as the absence of
the predicted group difference allows.

## A possible lexical influence on the response criterion

Where the lexicon may have left a mark was in how readily learners accepted gender-agreement
sentences. The Mini-Norwegian group's criterion
`r sdt_change_phrase("gender_agreement", "criterion", "Mini-Norwegian")` between Sessions 2
and 6, and in the reported models the difference from the Mini-English group was credible
`r sdt_language_clause("criterion")`. Once each learner's change in criterion was modelled,
the difference was credible `r sdt_language_clause_model("criterion", "_maxranef")` (see
*Strength of evidence*), so this section interprets a suggestive result. Read as accuracy,
this shift looks like an advantage, because a learner who accepts more sentences is right
more often on the grammatical ones. Read as signal detection, it is a change in willingness
to accept, unaccompanied by better discrimination. The shift appeared in the judgement and
not in the ERP response. If it is genuine, that places the group difference at the decision
more clearly than in the online processing of the violation, although the ERP estimates
were not precise enough to exclude a group difference in that processing.

Several mechanisms could produce such a shift, and the design does not separate them. One is
familiarity. Sentences that are processed more fluently are more readily endorsed as
grammatical in artificial grammar learning, particularly where knowledge is uncertain
[@scott2010; @topolinski2009]. Words built on Norwegian stems may be processed more fluently
by Norwegian speakers than words built on English stems, although we know of no study that
has shown lexical familiarity to shift the criterion in this way. A second is crosslinguistic
influence of a non-facilitative kind. If a Norwegian-like lexicon activates Norwegian
agreement patterns that do not match those of the miniature language, some violations would
look acceptable by Norwegian standards, raising false alarms and lowering sensitivity
together. That is the pattern the Linguistic Proximity Model calls misanalysis
[@westergaard2017], and it is consistent with the direction of the sensitivity difference,
`r sens_difference_concession()`. It could not arise from gender assignment,
because every noun takes the gender of its Norwegian equivalent in both languages (see
*Materials*), so no violation is licensed by a Norwegian assignment. For the same reason, an
item-level analysis relating false alarms to the Norwegian gender of each noun is not
available here: congruency is constant by construction, and the account can be tested only
in materials that cross it. A third is strategy.
Mini-English learners, facing gender marking that English lacks, may have scrutinised
agreement more cautiously. For differential object marking, the criterion changed between
Sessions 3 and 6 in both groups (Mini-Norwegian
`r report_sdt("differential_object_marking", "criterion", "change_first_to_last", "3->6", "Mini-Norwegian")`;
Mini-English
`r report_sdt("differential_object_marking", "criterion", "change_first_to_last", "3->6", "Mini-English")`),
and the between-language difference in that change was
`r report_sdt("differential_object_marking", "criterion", "change_first_to_last_language_difference", "3->6")`.
A familiarity account that operates on the lexicon as a whole should affect every property,
so whether the other properties show the same direction of difference bears on the first
mechanism.

The pattern also clarifies what the closest precedent found. @gonzalezalonso2020 observed a
group difference at first exposure in the ERP response but not in judgement accuracy, and
attributed it to how attention was allocated, a precursor of selecting a source, not to
grammatical processing. Their accuracy measure, like ours before we separated sensitivity
from criterion, could not have shown a criterion difference as such. Here, after training,
the lexical manipulation did not credibly alter the ERP grammaticality effect, and in the
reported models it moved the decision criterion. In both studies, then, the lexicon left
more trace in how learners engaged with the task than in their sensitivity to the grammar,
although here that trace is suggestive.

## Relation to the initial-exposure antecedent

Against @gonzalezalonso2020, these data replicate the general profile but not its specifics.
Their learners produced no P600 to gender-agreement violations at first exposure, and neither
did ours at any session. The dominant signature for gender agreement here was a violation
negativity, under a comparable artificial-language paradigm. The measurement occasion was not
comparable, since their ERPs come from a single first-exposure session, whereas ours begin
after the first training session, whose post-training test was repeated once when a learner
scored below 80%, and continue across four sessions. An early negativity to
gender-agreement violations was present in both studies. Their negativity was confined to
the English-lexicon group and to right-anterior electrodes, whereas ours was not credibly
modulated by language in any window. Their Spanish-lexicon group showed a broad positivity to
violations at 300--600 ms, whereas in our gender-agreement data the ungrammatical trials were
the more negative-going.

The divergences admit two kinds of explanation, and the literature on replication cautions
against reaching for the substantive kind first. Substantively, the designs differ in the
first language (Spanish against Norwegian), in the realisation of gender (concord across the
noun phrase against a suffixed or free determiner with predicate-adjective agreement), and in
the measurement occasion. Statistically, their groups comprised 26 and 24 learners. Effects
that reach significance in samples of that size systematically overestimate their true
magnitude and can even carry the wrong sign [@gelmancarlin2014], the significance filter
makes published effects look more replicable than they are [@vasishth2018], and trial-level
measurement error can inflate as well as attenuate an observed effect in small samples
[@loken2017]. ERP effects compound the problem, since even systematic resampling finds the
magnitude, onset and scalp distribution of the P600 to vary widely across samples [@kim2024].
The level at which replication should be assessed is therefore the qualitative one, where
the two studies agree that early-stage learners of a miniature language respond to
morphosyntactic violations without a canonical P600, and that the lexical manipulation shows
itself in how learners engage with the task more than in their grammatical sensitivity. The
same arguments cut against over-reading any group-specific effect in our own data, as the
*Strength of evidence* section below does.

## Development, retention and the control properties

Behavioural sensitivity declined across sessions (@fig-sdt-by-language), whereas the
gender-agreement ERP grammaticality effect grew in the late window. The two measures are recorded on the same
trials, so the dissociation is informative. Each session adds a property, and a judgement
made against a larger grammar is harder even when the response to a given violation has
strengthened. Session 6 follows about four months without exposure, which would lower
sensitivity in the judgements more than a well-consolidated violation response. The design
cannot separate these explanations from a drift in how learners approached the task over
the sessions.

The control properties showed no credible ERP modulation by language during training. For
differential object marking, the grammaticality $\times$ session $\times$ language term was
credible in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language", "differential_object_marking")`
cells, and for verb--object number agreement in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language", "verb_object_number_agreement")`.
Neither property differed between the groups in behavioural sensitivity at any session,
although the estimated decline in sensitivity to differential object marking was the
smaller in the Mini-Norwegian group, a difference whose interval included zero in the
reported models (see Results).`r dom_sens_guard()` The one language-conditioned
ERP result for a control property concerns retention. In the refits that free the Session 6
step, the early differential-object-marking effect of the Mini-Norwegian group fell below its
training trend at Session 6, and the difference between the groups in that deviation was
credible in `r retfree_tally("differential_object_marking", "language_difference", "credible")`
cells, both on the midline. No account predicted it, it rests on a trend estimated from two
sessions, and it falls in the window where the stimulus difference before the critical word
could contribute, so we treat it as a candidate for replication and not as a finding about
transfer. Differences in how easily the two lexicons were learned, and chance variation
across the grid, remain possible sources.

Over the retention interval, the gender-agreement effect strengthened in the late window,
where it had grown during training, and the groups did not differ credibly in that change.
Because the linear specification carries the training trend across the gap, that
strengthening is the trend evaluated over the interval. The refits that free the Session 6
step show that the effect at Session 6 did not depart credibly from that trend in any
gender-agreement cell (midline 400--900 ms,
`r retfree_val("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_midline")`), in either group or in the
difference between them (`r ret_lang_diff(freed = TRUE)`), although they estimate the
departure too imprecisely to tell continued growth from a plateau. Behavioural sensitivity,
by contrast, fell over the same interval, and the groups did not differ in how far
(`r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "sensitivity", "change_s4_to_s6_language_difference", "4->6")`).
Training studies of this kind find violation responses that hold or grow over months without
exposure [@morganshort2012plos], and the offline interval here could allow the consolidation
such studies describe [@dudai2015; @davis2009], but the present data do not isolate it.

## What the multivariate analysis adds

In the decoding reported here, the univariate and multivariate analyses order the
three properties in broadly the same way. Gender agreement carries an amplitude effect
credible in `r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality", "gender_agreement")` cells and
`r dec_gender_sep_phrase()`. Verb--object number agreement carries neither. Differential object
marking carries separability that its pre-stimulus
baseline forbids us to read as a violation response. That agreement was not guaranteed,
because the two analyses ask different questions. Window-averaged amplitude asks whether a condition shifts the mean
at a set of electrodes, whereas decoding asks whether the joint sensor pattern separates
single trials [@hebart2018; @wang2024]. A divergence in either direction would not have told
us which property is better represented, and classification accuracy is in any case not a
standardised effect size and cannot be compared across properties as though it were
[@hebart2018]. One limit is worth setting out before the mechanisms. Rejecting a
pooled cluster null licenses only that a grammaticality pattern is decodable in some part
of the sample, leaving its prevalence across participants unestimated [@allefeld2016].

Both profiles that can set the two analyses apart have documented mechanisms. A contrast can be decodable with
little univariate effect because decoding tolerates non-uniform response signs, so
neighbouring sensors of opposite polarity both carry information where averaging cancels
them [@hebart2018]. Forward modelling shows that such cancellation is substantial at the
scalp for distributed sources with partly opposing orientations [@ahlfors2010]. The
transient mean amplitude and comparatively high classification of differential object
marking are therefore compatible with a single generator whose spatial configuration is
stable even where its net amplitude is small, so far as the baseline difference allows
that reading. Multivariate analyses of sentence processing have repeatedly
recovered effects that the corresponding ERPs did not [@he2024; @cho2025]. The converse
profile is equally well characterised. Multivariate tests draw their sensitivity from
electrode-level variability in the effect within participants and are insensitive
to the between-participant variance in mean amplitude that governs univariate group
tests [@davis2014, on fMRI voxels], and increased
trial-to-trial variability leaves expected mean amplitude unchanged while progressively
shrinking expected decoding accuracy [@carrasco2024]. An effect that is consistent in
sign but spatially homogeneous would therefore yield a credible amplitude effect
with comparatively little for a classifier to exploit.`r dec_gender_profile_sentence()` Decoding is usually the more sensitive test of
the two, but it is not uniformly so, and comparable orderings are documented for the
mismatch negativity and the N2pc [@carrasco2024].

These considerations constrain the claims available to us. A failure to decode is a failure
to find linearly separable information under one analysis, and it leaves open whether the
brain distinguishes the conditions [@peelen2023]. Classification performance, high or low, is
a poor guide to representational content [@ritchie2019]. Nor would a divergence between the
two analyses support a conclusion about the dimensionality of the underlying code
[@davis2014].

The weak cross-property generalisation bears on a live theoretical question. If the
grammaticality response were largely a domain-general salience or integration signal
[@sassenhagen2019; @aurnhammer2023], a decoder trained on one property should transfer to
the others, but no direction exceeded a peak AUC of `r xprop_max()`, and with no null
distribution that value cannot be told apart from chance. That pattern is consistent with evidence
that the late positivity fractionates topographically and functionally [@kaan2003], that
agreement features follow separable developmental courses [@alemanbanon2018], that
different violation types within the same learners are predicted by different
individual-difference variables [@nichols2019], and that decoders of
grammatical features generalise selectively [@cho2025]. Reliable
cross-context transfer of linear EEG decoders is achievable [@zhao2025], which weighs
against reading the present result as simple insensitivity. Even so, failed
cross-classification is confounded with feature selection, since the sensors and
latencies that best separate grammatical from ungrammatical trials within a property need
not be those carrying a property-general signal [@kaplan2015]. We therefore read the
result as consistent with construction-specific coding, without taking it to refute any
shared component. A Bayes-factor treatment of the decoding time-course would
allow such nulls to be quantified as well as reported [@keysers2020;
@teichmann2022].

## Strength of evidence

The conclusions above should be read on the graded scale set out under *Inference*
[@makowski2019; @kruschke2018]. The central finding is an absence, and absences need their
precision stated. In the ERP models, the interval for the grammaticality $\times$ language
term for gender agreement is wide relative to the grammaticality effect itself (no bound
beyond `r term_max_bound("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language", "gender_agreement")`
within-participant standard deviations; compare the first and second rows of @fig-erp-forest), so the ERP data cannot exclude a language difference
of the size of the effect they measure, and they add little to the judgements on this point.
In the judgements, the sensitivity difference is also imprecisely estimated (averaged over
sessions, `r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "sensitivity", "language_difference", "average")`),
so the behavioural evidence against a Mini-Norwegian advantage rests more on its direction
than on its precision. We did not adopt an equivalence criterion, so neither null is a demonstration
that the groups are equivalent [@amrhein2019; @kruschke2018].

The criterion difference for gender agreement is the result that most needs qualifying. In
the reported models it was credible at
`r sdt_credible_sessions("gender_agreement", "criterion")` and grew
between Sessions 2 and 6. The refit that adds a by-participant slope for the change in bias
moved its estimates by no more than `r crit_maxranef_shift()` on the logit scale but widened
their intervals, and in that refit the difference was credible
`r sdt_language_clause_model("criterion", "_maxranef")`, nor did it grow credibly
(averaged over sessions,
`r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "criterion", "language_difference", "average", model = "accuracy_gender_agreement_maxranef")`;
growth between Sessions 2 and 6,
`r report_sdt("gender_agreement", "criterion", "change_first_to_last_language_difference", "2->6", model = "accuracy_gender_agreement_maxranef")`).
That slope lets each learner's criterion change at its own rate, and leaving it out can make
the interval of the corresponding fixed effect too narrow [@barr2013], which is why the ERP
models carry its counterpart. The direction of the difference is the same in every fit,
`r crit_direction_clause()`, but its credibility depends on the random-effect structure, and
we grade it as suggestive.`r maxranef_claims_guard()`

`r rtscreen_weight_paragraph()`

The gender-agreement ERP learning effect is credible in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session", "gender_agreement")` cells under
the maximal random-effect structure and in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session", "gender_agreement", structure = "base")`
without the by-item slope, and the same cells stay credible under the weak priors and without
the reprocessed and recovered records. It is confined to the late window, however, and the
interval of its midline estimate lies close to zero, so we grade it as clear in direction but
modest in size. The one language-conditioned ERP result, the deviation at retention in two
early differential-object-marking cells, is unpredicted and confined to two of the twelve
cells in which it was estimated, and we grade it as suggestive. The retention estimates rest
on the participants who returned for Session 6 and are graded no higher.

The decoding evidence grades separately.`r dec_gender_grade_sentence()` Differential
object marking's `r dec_count(dec_dom, "n_overall_fdr", "cluster")` begin before the
critical word, and the word before it differs between the conditions, so no part of its
separability can be attributed to a violation response. The session-resolved breakdowns enter no correction
family and are descriptive. Several features of the analysed sample were fixed after the
models had first been fitted, and all are set out under *Transparency, preregistration and
analysis status*: the reprocessing of nine Session 3 recordings filtered at 1 Hz, the
recovery of two of three mislabelled exports and the exclusion of the third, and the
exclusion of a participant trained in the wrong miniature language at Session 2. The
robustness analysis that leaves out the reprocessed and recovered records changes no ERP
conclusion (@tbl-robustness).

## Limitations and future directions

The strongest constraint on what this design can conclude is that the miniature languages
were built to probe the lexicon's role at first exposure, and the transfer accounts do not
make mutually exclusive predictions for most of what the design measures once learning is
under way. Only gender agreement has a first-language analogue, and for it the accounts
separate only on the absence of a Mini-Norwegian advantage. Three additions would sharpen the
test. A measurement before any training would capture the initial state that the Typological
Primacy Model constrains. A group whose first language lacks gender, learning the same
miniature languages, would show whether Norwegian facilitated gender agreement at all, and so
whether the L2 Status Factor can be separated from property-by-property accounts. Crossing the
lexicon with the position of the gender-marking determiner would separate the lexical cue from
the structural one, which the present languages confound [@jensen2023; @castle2026].

Several further features of the design constrain the conclusions. The properties enter at
different sessions, so a property's identity is confounded with its amount of exposure, and
cross-property comparisons are not exposure-matched. Assignment to language followed a fixed
rule on the participant identifier, so the groups were not formed by random allocation. The
post-training test was repeated once for a learner who scored below 80% at the first attempt,
after which every learner continued, so the first ERP session follows a variable amount of
training. Additional gendered or case-marking languages reported under *Participants* were
not screened out. Such experience could support the gender or marking structures, and it is
only partly absorbed by the L1-dominance covariate, which enters the ERP models only. Of the
`r flow_n("enrolled")` learners enrolled, `r flow_n("attended_S6")` attended the retention
test, so the Session 6 estimates draw on the returners, who may differ from those who left.
Effects are quantified as mean amplitudes in fixed latency windows, and without a
native-speaker baseline the native-likeness of the developing response is untested.`r trigger_limit_sentence()` Each
sentence frame belongs to one miniature language, so a difference between the groups'
judgements is also a difference between two sets of frames, which a by-item term can
absorb but no design that keeps the lexicons apart can remove. Cognitive individual-difference predictors are
analysed in a companion paper [@lesspredictors2026].

## Conclusion

Norwegian--English bilinguals learning a Norwegian-like miniature language were no more
sensitive to its gender agreement than learners of an English-like one, although gender is a
Norwegian property that English lacks. Their judgements showed no sensitivity advantage at
any session, and their ERP response showed no group difference either, though it could not
exclude one. That absence is what property-by-property accounts of transfer allow and what
the Typological Primacy Model, which predicts that the lexicon selects the grammar, does
not. The lexicon may have left its mark on the decision instead. In the later sessions,
Mini-Norwegian learners accepted gender-agreement sentences more readily, ungrammatical ones
included, but that difference was not credible once each learner's change in criterion was
modelled. The design cannot show that Norwegian helped either group or recover the initial
state, so the transfer debate is narrowed and not settled. What the results establish is
that a Norwegian-like lexicon brought no advantage in sensitivity to a Norwegian property.
Whether it shaped how learners engaged with the task is a question for a design built to
test it.

# Data and code availability

Data extraction, model fitting and reporting are fully scripted as a reproducible
research compendium [@marwick2018]. Models were fitted on High-Performance Computing
(HPC) clusters at Sigma2 (Norway) and the University of Oxford's Advanced Research
Computing facility, on Linux (`r prov("platform", "*[platform pending a pipeline run]*")`)
under R `r prov("R")` [@rcoreteam], with `brms` `r prov("brms")` [@burkner2017] driving
CmdStan `r prov("CmdStan")` through the `cmdstanr` `r prov("cmdstanr")` backend. The clusters
supply that stack through environment modules, with no container. The compiler settings
used on those clusters are recorded in the repository and do not change the models.
Every version given here comes from the provenance record the fitting run wrote. Model
fitting used the fixed seed `r prov("seed:LES_SEED", "*[seed pending a pipeline run]*")`, set in the shared
Bayesian settings and recorded in that provenance record. Each chain evaluated the likelihood
in parallel (`reduce_sum`), which groups its partial sums at run time, so a rerun with the
same seed reproduces the posterior summaries to within Monte Carlo error, not draw for draw.
`r sdt_mcse_sentence()` The decoding permutations used
the seed `r prov_dec("seed:LES_DECODE_SEED", as.character(LES_P1_DECODE_SEED_DEFAULT))`,
`r if (is.null(.dprov_tbl)) "the default the decoding scripts set" else "exported by the job script that runs them and recorded by that script beside the decoding artefacts"`.
This manuscript reads only the script-generated summary tables,
so every statistic in the Results is populated from them and none is transcribed by hand.
The pooled posterior summaries, retention contrasts, convergence diagnostics, sample-flow
counts and decoding time-courses that populate the figures and tables are all published
with the repository. The decoding artefacts include the participant count behind every
per-cell score. Figures are drawn with `ggplot2` [@wickham2016]
using the theme and colour system of `depictr` [@depictr], whose default qualitative
palette is the colourblind-safe Okabe--Ito set. The companion paper [@lesspredictors2026]
uses the same system, so the two share one visual identity. The literature counts in
@fig-literature
were retrieved from the Scopus Search API with `scopusflow` [@scopusflow], which records
the exact query beside each count, so the search is reproducible from the repository. Its
coverage limits are stated in the figure note. All extraction, modelling and reporting
scripts, the script-generated summary tables and the environment specification are
available at <https://github.com/pablobernabeu/LESS-morphosyntactic-transfer>. The
environment specification comprises an `renv` lockfile pinning the R packages of the
fitting library and a provenance record written at fit time. That record holds the software versions in force
when the ERP models were fitted, which is what the versions above are read from. The
accuracy models and the decoding analyses run in the same cluster environment under
separate scripts. The accuracy script records the R, brms, cmdstanr and CmdStan versions
of each fit in the pooled fit metadata that accompanies the results, and the decoding job
records its seed and permutation settings beside the decoding artefacts. The raw
electroencephalographic recordings, too large to distribute through an ordinary
version-control repository, and the raw behavioural logs are openly available in the
project's Open Science Framework repository at <https://osf.io/tq7vy>.

# Analytic decisions in detail {#apx-analytic-decisions-in-detail}

This appendix sets out the reasoning behind three analytic choices that the Method states
but does not argue in full: the retention of the by-item grammaticality slope in the ERP
models, the treatment of the recordings filtered at 1 Hz and of the mislabelled exports, and
the definition of the false-discovery-rate correction family for the decoding analyses. It
also reports a check on the trials that the segmentation's trigger rule discards.

## The by-item grammaticality slope

The reason for keeping the by-item grammaticality slope is that dropping it would bias the
test in the direction of the hypothesis. @barr2013 show that omitting random-effect
structure that is present in the population inflates the Type I error rate. They add that,
for within-items manipulations specifically, an intercept-only by-item structure can inflate
it severely, whatever method is used to obtain $p$-values or intervals. Grammaticality is a
within-item manipulation here, so an item term carrying only an intercept and a session
slope is exactly that case for the effect under test.

@matuschek2017 argue the other side: a maximal model can cost power, and they recommend
reducing to a structure the data support. We report the maximal structure nonetheless, for
two reasons. Their argument is that a maximal structure the data do not support costs power, a
result they establish in simulations of models that converge, so it does not turn on
convergence failure. They themselves note that maximal models usually do converge when
fitted in a Bayesian framework such as Stan, while explicitly leaving open whether
fitting overparameterised maximal models makes sense there. Every cell of our reported
grid converged under the maximal structure, on the same criteria as under the reduced one.
The retention-free refits are diagnosed separately in @apx-convergence-diagnostics, where
any fit that missed a criterion is marked. We also fit the whole grid a second time without the
by-item grammaticality slope, so a reader can see which conclusions depend on it. That
comparison follows.

## Sensitivity to the by-item grammaticality slope

To show what the maximal structure buys, we refitted the whole grid without the by-item
grammaticality slope, the structure a design in which grammaticality varied only within
participants would have justified. `r struct_conv_sentence()`

In these data, the choice matters little. Posterior medians barely move between the two
structures, and at the median the maximal structure's intervals are
`r itemslope_width_ratio("z_recoded_grammaticality")` times the simpler structure's width
for the grammaticality main effect and `r itemslope_width_ratio()` times for the
grammaticality $\times$ session $\times$ language interaction. The credible cells are the
same under both for the grammaticality main effect
(`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality", structure = "itemslope")` cells under the
maximal structure against `r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality", structure = "base")`
without the slope), for the grammaticality $\times$ session interaction
(`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session", structure = "itemslope")`
against `r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session", structure = "base")`)
and for the three-way interaction
(`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language", structure = "itemslope")`
against
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language", structure = "base")`).
The one difference is in the grammaticality $\times$ language interaction for differential
object marking in the early lateral window, which is credible without the by-item slope
(`r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_200_500_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language", exact = TRUE)`)
and falls just short of credibility with it
(`r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_200_500_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language")`),
so that the count is
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language", structure = "itemslope")`
cells against
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language", structure = "base")`.`r cred_agree_guard("", "_itemslope", differ = "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language")`
No conclusion rests on that cell. By-item variability in the grammaticality response is
therefore small in these data, and the case for the maximal structure rests on the argument
of the previous section, not on what it changes here.

## The reprocessed recordings and the mislabelled exports

The Session 3 recordings of nine participants were high-pass filtered at 1 Hz where every
other recording was filtered at 0.1 Hz. Four were identified when the analysis was first
assembled and five more when the archived processing histories of every recording were
audited. One further history, of a Session 2 recording, also reads 1 Hz, but its settings
were edited after the export was written: rebuilt from the raw data, that export is
reproduced only at 0.1 Hz, so it is used as it stands. We did not assess whether these
participants' data look unusual, and the treatment of the 1 Hz data does not rest on that.
It rests on the setting itself, which is a documented generator of artefacts in this kind of
paradigm. Filtering data from a syntactic- and semantic-violation experiment at cutoffs of
0.3 Hz and above introduces spurious deflections of opposite polarity immediately before the
true N400 and P600 effects [@tanner2015], and 1 Hz lies well inside that range. The general
principle, that a high-pass cutoff must be matched to the analysis window because an
inappropriate one generates artefactual slow deflections, is set out by @widmann2015.
Because the decision follows from the filter's known behaviour, and nothing observed in these
participants bore on it, it is not a results-contingent choice.

Pooling the 1 Hz data with the rest would be the wrong remedy, because a distortion that
precedes and reshapes the component of interest does not cancel in the difference between
conditions [@tanner2015]. Excluding them would remove about a sixth of the Session 3 ERP
trials, and four or five participants from each group at that session. The raw continuous
recordings of all nine sessions are archived, so they were instead reprocessed at 0.1 Hz,
under a protocol fixed before any reprocessed output was inspected. The archived processing
was first reconstructed by script and shown to reproduce every existing 1 Hz export to within
the rounding of the export, and only then was the high-pass cutoff changed, with every other
step and every retained trial kept as archived. The reprocessed data enter the primary
analysis, and their exclusion is the single sensitivity analysis. That analysis can qualify a
primary result but never create one, so running it adds no opportunity for a false positive.
A primary ERP result counts as sample-sensitive if, without the reprocessed and recovered
records, its median changes sign or its interval no longer excludes zero in the primary
direction. @tbl-robustness sets the two analyses side by side for every grammaticality term,
and @tbl-retention-robustness does the same for the Session 4 to Session 6 contrasts. No
primary ERP result is sample-sensitive by that rule. No grammaticality term becomes credible
without the reprocessed and recovered records that was not credible with them, and one
retention contrast does, as reported in the Results; under the protocol it cannot become a
claim.`r cred_agree_guard("_exclreproc_itemslope", "_itemslope")``r ret_robust_guard(extra = "erp_gender_agreement_400_900_midline within_Mini-English")`

The same audit traced every exported trial to its source recording and checked every
export for a stimulus-locked response, and three exports failed. The Session 3 export of one
Mini-Norwegian participant was produced from another Mini-Norwegian participant's Session 3
recording, so it duplicates that participant's data: the two exports share every trial time
stamp, and trials paired by time stamp correlate closely at the posterior midline, whereas
trials of different participants do not. The Session 6 export of one Mini-English
participant was cut at the event times of that participant's Session 4 recording, and the
Session 2 export of another Mini-English participant at the event times of a recording other
than the one archived. The epochs of both are not time-locked to any stimulus: the
average over their trials shows no reliable evoked response, and does not resemble the
other participants' averages, whereas the same participants' other sessions show clear
evoked responses. Unlike the filter setting, which distorts a real response, these exports
contain no response of the participant-session they are named for, so no analysis can
use them as they stand. A misaligned record can be recovered if its archived inspection and
ocular correction were made on its own EEG, with only its event times wrong. The protocol
tests that by first reproducing the legacy export from the archived recording, and only then
re-segments the record at its own events. Both misaligned records passed. In each, the
processing history had been built on the participant's own recording, within a stretch of it
that the analyst had marked out, and only the event markers had come from another recording.
The re-segmentation keeps that stretch, since outside it no epoch received any inspection, so
31 of the 144 condition events of the Session 2 record, which precede it, are not used. The
recovered records enter the primary analysis and are left out of the robustness analysis with
the reprocessed ones. The duplicated Session 3 record cannot be recovered, because every
processing decision behind it was made on the other participant's recording, and it stays
excluded.

```{r}
#| include: false
# Side-by-side tables of the primary fits and the robustness refits that leave out the
# reprocessed and recovered records (LES_P1_EXCLUDE_REPROCESSED=1, model ids tagged
# "_exclreproc"). The reprocessing protocol requires every primary and robustness estimate to
# be reported together, including where the conclusion is unchanged. Both families are the
# maximal structure under the informative priors, the only specification the robustness
# analysis refits. `d` holds the rows of both families; `key` names the column that carries
# the row quantity (a model term or a retention contrast) and `labs` maps its values to row
# labels in display order. Precision is one .les_digits value for the whole table.
.robust_table <- function(d, key, labs, head) {
  d <- d[grepl("^erp_.*_(lateral|midline)(_exclreproc)?_itemslope$", d$model) &
           d[[key]] %in% names(labs), , drop = FALSE]
  if (!nrow(d) || !any(grepl("_exclreproc", d$model))) return(NULL)
  d$rob  <- grepl("_exclreproc_itemslope$", d$model)
  d$cell <- sub("(_exclreproc)?_itemslope$", "", d$model)
  m <- regmatches(d$cell, regexec("^erp_(.+?)_([0-9]+)_([0-9]+)_(lateral|midline)$", d$cell))
  part <- function(j) vapply(m, function(x) if (length(x)) x[j] else NA_character_, "")
  d$Property <- factor(unname(LES_PROPERTY_LABELS_TABLE[part(2)]),
                       levels = unname(LES_PROPERTY_LABELS_TABLE))
  d$w1  <- as.integer(part(3))
  d$Sub <- paste0(part(3), "–", part(4), " ms, ", part(5))
  d$Key <- factor(d[[key]], levels = names(labs))
  f <- .fmt_est(d$median, d$ci_low, d$ci_high)
  d$Mdn <- f$median; d$LL <- f$lo; d$UL <- f$hi
  keys <- unique(d[, c("Property", "w1", "Sub", "Key")])
  keys <- keys[order(keys$Property, keys$w1, keys$Sub, keys$Key), , drop = FALSE]
  body <- data.frame(Row = .les_keep(unname(labs[as.character(keys$Key)]),
                                     paste(keys$Property, keys$Sub)),
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  for (fam in c(FALSE, TRUE)) for (col in c("Mdn", "LL", "UL"))
    body[[paste(fam, col)]] <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(keys)), function(i) {
      x <- d[[col]][d$rob == fam & d$Property == keys$Property[i] & d$Sub == keys$Sub[i] &
                      d$Key == keys$Key[i]]
      if (length(x) == 1L) x else "—"
    }, "")
  les_grid_table(body,
    header   = .les_widths(c(head, rep(c("*Mdn*", "*LL*", "*UL*"), 2)),
                           pdf = c(.34, rep(.11, 6)), docx = c(.34, rep(.11, 6))),
    align    = c("l", rep("r", 6)),
    spanners = list(list(label = "Primary", cols = 2:4),
                    list(label = "Without reprocessed", cols = 5:7)),
    group    = .les_group(as.character(keys$Property)),
    subgroup = .les_group(keys$Sub, italic = FALSE))
}
```
